INDEPENDENT LABOUR PARTY.

when those of them who were now young were crippled with the usages of time and bent under the weight of years, they might be enabled to took back on past days with pride and pleasure and hard on to their children's children a rich and glorious harvest of a great dull absorbing faith. div.head: Salo ol Work at Warrington.
div.p: Salo ol Work at Warrington.

What were pleasantly termed capitalistic methods of raising funds were adopted by the ‘Varrington branch of the Independent Labour Party on Saturday when a sale of work was held in the Gymnasium, Palmyra Square. Considerable interest was taken in the project by looal members and supporters of the party and there was a good attendance at the opening ceremony which was performed by Mr. T. Russell Williams, who recently contested Huddersfield unsuccessfully in the Socialist interest. Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P. presided. The hymn" England arise" having been sung, Coun- cillor STOTT, in introducing Mr. Seddon, said they had to use the methods employed by capitalists and they were about to exploit not only themselves but; the people of Warrington for support. In other words,they were going to use capitalistic methods so as to be in a better position to break down capitalism. (Applause.) Mr. SEDDON, M.P., said he had no doubt many of those present were anxious to get rid of their super- abundant wealth—(laughter)—and the stall-holders would be willing to relieve them of that responsibility. That bazaar was being held for the purpose of securing farther financial help for the spread of Socialism. It had been jocularly said that everybody were Socialists to-day, but actually that was not true. They had the 'greatest fight in front of them that the movement had ever had. The forces against them were organizing themselves. They were becornieg alarmed and imagined that destruction was going to overtake them, and that violence was going to overtake the country. It was therefore highly important that Socialists should allay suspicion by re-stating their principles. So far as they were concerned, they said they were not destroyers but believiers in evolution. Society to-day contained the germs of its own destruction. It was self-condemned and unless it was possible for the mind of man to conceive something better and nobler society would not progress but recede and finally we would become victims of the law of the jungle. The Socialist movement was not peculiar for the opposition it had engendered. Every great reformer in the world's 'history had been per- secuted first and very often worshipped afterwards. Even the lowly Nazarene was opposed and crucified by the very people who professed to honour Him and place Him in the high position He occupied in the thoughts and hearts of men to-day. Therefore Socialists were not alarmed at the growing opposition. They said that inherently the principles they held were the only hope of the workers in this and every other land; and they approximated nearest to the dreams of all the philosophers and poets of the ages that had gone. Socialists claimed that there were only two sources of wealth—mother Nature, and labour applied. That being so, there was no justification in laws either human or Divine, for the present state of anarchy. We had been blessed by Providence with wealth, enough and to spare and yet we had the appalling problem confronting us that under increased methods of wealth production we were only creating a few million- aires on the one side and condemning millions to poverty from the cradle to the grave. That was not the right conception of human life. The highest conception must always be that of brotherhood, where each would give according to his ability and each receive according to his need. Socialists contended that their principles were in accordance with the highest conception of human duty—the realization of brotherhood one towards the other. The object of that bazaar was to show in a practical manner their sympathy with the mckement in Warrington. There were a few amongst amongst them who had been in the fore-front for long years. They had carried the banner aloft and he was glad to think they were seeing the fruition of their, work in the education of the young and the adherents who were coming into the movement in Warrington. He asked his hearers to give those old workers further heart by letting them see that the new adherents were just as enthusiastic as they themselves hadbeen lathe days of darkness. The proceeds of that sale would not only encourage them but would provide the sinews of war to continue the propaganda until the time came when Socialism was the aceepted doctrine of the whole of the people and not of the few. (Applause.) Mr. RussELL Wsussais expressed the great pleasure it afforded him to be once again in Warrington. The last time he and Mr. Seddon met,'Mr. Seddon misdoing his best to persuade the people of Huddersfield to record their votes in his (Mr. Williams') favour. The peculiar circumstance was that fewer votes were recorded for him on the last occasion than at the previous election, when he had it to himsel F. (Laughter.) He was not, however, saying there was any reflection to be cast on his workers in that matter. (Laughter.) The principles for which Socialists stood were in harmony with the greatest thoughts laid down for 'human consideration by the great philosophers who had gone before. He was glad that the recognition of that fact was spreading throughout the length ond breadth of the kingdom, but Lancashire had a long row to hoe before it came abreast of Yorkshire. There were more members of the I.L.P. within the boundaries of York- shire than in all the rest of England. The chvelopment of the Socialistic sentiment at Huddersfield made it necessary for them to make it a question: Shall the people accept Socialism or deny it for the nonce? They chose to deny it, but the work of pronaganda was going on. The I.L.P. was putting something like 27 propa- gandists in the field during the coming summer to spread the truths for which they stood and they were hoping to double the membership of the party by the end of the summer. They wanted each branch to pay a valuation fixed upon all its mem- bers, so that instead of raising 42,000 a year for a special effort fond they might obtain during the next year £4,000 or £5,000. They hoped, like trade unionists, to appoint permanent organiser!. He hoped that bazaar would be a success and that out of its success would grow a greater enthusiasm for the work inthat district. He sincerely hoped that all those who had become identified with the movement would continue to do what they could for the benefit of the cause and that they would not only be Socialists in principle but in practice, seeking to make the lives of their comrades better for their association with them. If that be so, he had not the slightest hesitation in pre- dicting that sometime in the dim and distant future,

Mr. J. Pendry acted as general secretary. • During the day there were three concerts, the pro- grammes submitted being highly interesting. The artistes were :—Miss Plinston (pianoforte solos and songs), Miss Hackett, Mr. R. Ray, Mr. J. Corrin, Mr. Percy Jaggard, Mr. Andy Griffin, Mr. Fred Roberts. Mr. Harry Lazenby, Mrs. Hannan (songs), Misses Wilkinson and Hewitt (dance), the "Merry Uns " (sketches). There were also some very amusing competitions. A hat-trimming contest attract.d 14 competitors, and Mrs. Lees awarded the prize to Mr. W. Whitely. There was also a nail-driving competition for ladies, 24 of whom took part. Mr. W. Rigby divided the prize between Mrs. Wolf and Mrs. Whitely. The sale was highly successful.

Over 44 years after Mrs. Welch, 27, Dolman's-lane, Warrington, told about her cure by Doan's backache kidney pills, she said :—" It is all quite true about the good Doan's pills did me some long time back, and I have had no return of the old troubles.My cure has proved a lasting one, and I am always glad to recommend the medicine that did so much for me."

Here are the details of Mrs. Welsh's case, given in a statement she made at the time of her cure You are quite welcome to publish my testimonial for Doan's backache kidney pills and I hope it will be the means of others trying the medicine. • "My ailment was kidney disorder, and the symptoms were bad pains in my back and loins, dimness of sight, giddiness, and urinary trouble. I was very low and feeble, and I had to take bold of the furniture when I moved about the house. Specks seemed to be floating before my eyes, and I felt full of wind. "I consulted a doctor, and he told me my kidneys were diseased,and I should have to be careful or dropsy would set in. He gave me some medicine, but I got no better, and as time went on I grew worse. "When I began with Doan's backache kidney pills I did not get much benefit from the first box, but I per- severed with the medicine, and with the second box I began to improve. Gradually the pains left "me, my sight became clearer, and the kidney secretions were natural. I have derived more relief from Doan's pills than from all the medicine I tried. I shall do what I can to reccoramend the pills." Doan's Backache Kidney Pills are two sbillings and ninepence per box (six boxes for thirteen shillings and ninepence). At the Spanish Court. —The style of cooking at the Spanish Court is French, with a consitierable admixture of Spanish and German dishes. The Royal kitchen is controlled by a Frenchman, and he has at his orders more than thirty helpers, the pastry cooks and ice- makers being Italians. Bteakfast is served punctually at eight o'clock, luncheon at half-past twelve, dinner at seven, and the menu is invariably written out in French. Except on grand occasions the dinner plate is of silver, and the wines usually served are sherry, Rioga-Riscal, and champagne. When the evening meal is over the labours of the Royal cook and his subordinates come to an end, and the servants doing night duty begin their work, which consists of sitting up all night in case any member of the Royal Family desires anything to eat or drink, a thing which occurs very seldom. The Lord Chamberlain and the Stage.—The office of the Lord Chamberlain as sole censor of plays, dates from the time of George IL, when the notion still survived that actors and actresses were all more or less rogues. There was frequently friction between the theatrical profession and the Lord Chamberlain, and the " Mikado ' incident has revived the demand for the reform of the office of censorship. The Lord Chamber- lain has absolute pover, there being no appeal against his decision, and the vesting of such autocratic powers in a high Court official, it is held is wrong and quite out of date. In view of the magnitude of the interests idvolved, the censorship, is is urged, should be vested in a specially constituted and qualified authority. The Queen of Nurses.—The celebration of her eighty- seventh birthday, by Miss Florence Nightingale, recalls the fact that she was one of the first to recognise that nursing was a calling for educated women. She want out to the Crimea 1854, but bfore that she bad done much by her example to elevate the nursing profession, which had hitherto been mostly.left to the class of persons represented by Sairey Gawp and Betsy Prig. The daughter of a wealthy country gentleman, she and her sister passed their childhood and youth most') at Lea Hurst, Derbyshire, and at Enably Park, Hampshire. At that period, not much attention was paid to the higher education, even amongst the country families. but Mr. Nightingale was an exception to the rule, and fortunately for the world, his daughter Florence was educated in advance of the majority gentlewomen of her time.

Dress on the River.—Those 'girls and women who intend spending time on the river this coming summer, will do well to bear in mind the fact, that hats are of primary importance. The lounger in the punt shows but little of the style of her gown, so that if it looks clean and trim that is about all that is necessary to gain a verdict of " attractive," but to deserve this she must crown herself with special care, appropriateness, and becomingnesa. In the matter of colours green looks cool and dainty, pink is effective, but red is best of all. A red parasol, and a red hat always looks extremely well, on the water, on a sunshiny day, indeed they look superlatively well, and nothinOcan beat them. The Craze for Pink.—During the past week or two there has been quite an epidemic of pink, all the windows of drapery establishments are sat out with pink fabrics, pink costumes are to the fore in the dress- makers show rooms, and pink is the leading colour at the milliners. Last year we had an epidemic of blue, pale blue, which as a rule proves infinitely more becom- ing than the present modish pink, even in the dull, soft tones so conspicuously in favour. Pale shades of green may be said to rank next to pink in our affections, just now, but here again great care needs to be exercised in the choice of the tone.

A Revival.—Throughout the winter we were putting applications of cloth on velvet, voiles, chiffons, and even lace, and the idea seems to have "caught on " again now that summer frocks are under consideration, for many of the new canvas dresses shew applications of plain linen, and again linen tailor-mades are trimmed with canvas. Scroll applications matching in colour, the foundation, are preferred at the moment, the scrolls being outlined with a lighter or darker shade.

How to Pack Flowers.—Flowers destined to travel, should be cut in the early morning, before the sun is upon them, and the stems should be immediately placed in cold water. About an hour before pecking tepid water should be substituted for the cold, and when lay- ing the blooms in the box care should be taken that each stem is separated from all others by means of cotton wool or waxed paper. If the foregoing simple procedure is followed, the most delicate flowers should come out perfectly fresh even after a journey of several hours.

Out-door Cushions.—All cushions intended for garden seats or chairs, should be covered on one side with thin American cloth. This side should always be turned uppermost when the cushions are not in use, so that in the event of a sudden Shower they may not become wet through. With regard to the ornamental side, a desir- able plan is not to choose excessively bright colours, as those are very apt to rub off, and soil delicate dresses, moreover very glaring hues are all too liable to " kill " dainty toilettes.
MADGE.

div.head: "THE EVERLASTING HILLS."
div.p: "THE EVERLASTING HILLS."

Hail, glorious hills, ye heights sublime, Whose summits seem to touch the sky; Ye silent sentinels of time, That mark the ages rolling by! Still onward with a ceaseless flow, Time speeds to an eternal shore; And lays man's puny fabrics low In ruin whence they rise no more. But all in vain have years and storms Against ye all their powers essayed; Still rise your everlasting forms In all their pristine strength arrayed. And down beneath the ocean's bed Your adamantine roots extend; And round its shores your ramparts spread, from rolling waves our homes defend. And when with wondering eyes we trace Your rugged cliffs and outlines fair, What glory rests on every place, What marks of power Almighty there ! Then in your shadows, wondrous bills, What valleys smile beneath the sun; While noble streams and tiny rills Through all their lovely windings run. And 0, when from your summits lone, Heaven's arch is seen when night is clear, Less distant seems the starry zone, More brilliant far its gems appear! J. IL W. CLINDINNING. -

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
THE MARRYING AGE.

scientific journal has been dealing with the subject of the marrying age for women, a deli- cate one to handle at all times. But we can all see for ourselves nowadays, says a ladies' paper, that the tendency is to marry lato rather than early, and, therefore, woman has to be viewed from an entirely different standpoint than hew- tofote. And as our medical contemporary re- marks, it therefore has become incumbent upon women to cultivate attractions of an order which would have once set the seal of "old-maidism" upon their sex a generation or two •ago. The old stock-in-trade of youth and beauty, it is said, are no longer essential., Of far greater market- able value are a practieal mind, level-headedness tact, and a smart' appearance. And it is sug- gested that the most successful -,woman of the new marriageable type is sho who, while she dresses well, neither accentuates her ago nor adopts subterfuges to appear more youthful than she is.

div.head: WHITE LIES,
div.p: WHITE LIES,

The idea of a "blameless double life" can hardly be put forward as novel, says "Miranda" in the La6's Piciorial. Our whole social system has, been built' up in this way. The most amiable, virtuous, single-minded of tiq are forced to lead double lives, at least during some moments of each day, and while we have to resort to tho duplicity of the " white lie" it cannot well be otherwise. The hostess who sits in her boudoir and is "not at home" is a standard instance of the "double life" which I admittedly blameless, if baffling.

div.head: SERGE COSTUME.
div.p: SERGE COSTUME.

Our illustration shews a smart costume of deep cream serge. The full skirt is finished at the hem with a stitched strap of the material, ar- ranged with short upstanding straps at intervals. The fronts of the short coat har,g loose, but at the sides and back it is given a short-waisted appearance by a stitched strap, and is finished

with a short, pleated basque. The corfar is faced with almond-green velvet, and outlined with a narrow strapping of serge, the fronts being de- corated with loops of braid and cream silk cords. The sleeves are drawn in close to the arm at the elbow, and aro arranged with a stitched tab, which is finished with loops of cord attached'to mether-o'-pearl buttons set in gilt rims.
DRESS AND THE WEARER

Many charming gowns where simplicity is the foremost note are spoilt by additions made by the ,wearer, writes "I-leloise" in the Lady. Some women have not the " instinct" of colour, though others know, exactly how to emphasise the charm of a plain or simple toilet. You will see a black cloth costume worn in different ways, although both gowns are identical. In one case the black gown is voted dowdy, and colour is added recklessly: an Oriental vest, a knot "of pink carnations, and a coloured hat. Treated in this fashion, the black gown becomes common- place, and the wearer certainly acquires no dis- tinction from her setting. But worn with a white vest with cascades of creamy lace, a simple black hat, relieved slightly with cream or ivory, and a white fur or feather boa, the most ordi- nary black gown becomes quite passable, and, with the addition of long white gloves and a cluster of lilies-of-the-valley or pale pink carna- tions, presents quite a smart appearance. Some women, again, never dream of wearing a silk tie or a lace scarf, and miss the charm of con- trast and colour. Take, for instance, a blouse of white embroidered linen, which certainly looks fresh and dainty on its first appearance, but in nineteen out of twenty cases is far front becom- ing to its wearer. Add a scarf of cherry-coloured or royal-blue silk and a narrow turned-down collar of tinted lace or la*n, and you prevent the dead white tint from being in close proximity to the face, and, without affecting the dainti- ness, add the necessary touch which makes it becoming. __

div.head: USEFUL WALKING-SKIRT.
div.p: USEFUL WALKING-SKIRT.

I always consider—and I think that most of my readers will agree with me—that a smart short walking-skirt is quite one of the most use- ful garments in the summer wardrobe. Just such a skirt is illustrated in our sketch, and;..it is, I assure you, of the very latest and smartest type, the immense width at the hem giving it a jaunty swing at the feet which is most bewitching. This

skirt is made with a succession of box-pleats arranged at intervals all round, and firmly machined down to a point a little below the hip. Between these -pl:sats come groups of flat, stitched tucks, each group held in place by pointed bands of the material, machined at the edges and placed a few inches apart. Below these bands the tucks are • released, being allowed to hang loosely to the hem.

div.head: HOW TO HOLD UP A GOWN.
div.p: HOW TO HOLD UP A GOWN.

It is astonishing, • remarks the Queen, how many women spoil. .their appearance by ignor- ance of the simple art of holding up the skirt with something approaching to grace. It is quite impossible to let the hem sweep the path- way. Paris women know how to do this to per- fection, and the frilled skirts and dainty cha.seures add to their charms. The best plan is to gather the fulness on one side just where .the hand would naturally fall, drawing the folds for- ward. and by this means the front of the skirt is raised straight. The grasp should be light in order to avoid creases. The left hand should be used. Care should be taken not to draw the drapery so tight that the ,outline of the figure .is umgracefully• held.

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE,
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE,

CREAM or BEET SOUP. One quart of beets, one quart of milk, one tablespoonful of butter, two tablespoonfuls of flour. Scrape the skin from the beets, and put them on to boil in a pint of water. Cook until 'tender, when the water in which they were boiled should be of a deep crimson hue.. Chop the beets, and press them through a vegetable press, then add them to the xvater Cook toirether in a saucepan the butter Waal Hour, and when they mime scir slowiy on them the scalding milk. Stir over the fire until the mixture thickens, then add the beet puree. Season with salt and white pepper. • If properly prepared, this soup will be rose pink in colour, and very pretty.

"Well, we must find out whether the in- spector has been picked up or not, for he is cute enough to keep the kidnapping of him- self out of the papers, so that we may learn nothing from that source. The best thing you can do is to go disguised to Scotland Yard and ask for him. You know Pan, the Austrian Anarchist? Well, he now has a dirty restaurant in Soho. The man de- dounced a fellow-conspirator in Vienna to save his own skin, got two hundred pounds reward, escaped to England, and set up in Soho under another name. As he has been there two years no doubt he thinks himself safe. Your business is to denounce him to the inspector, for he is wanted for another crime. Give no reason, simply denounce him as Pan, and the inspector will understand. There is an extradition warrant out in all European cities for him, and a reward offered. As I happen to have a regard for the man he de- nounced there is reason enough for me, and it will serve our turn to find out the truth as to that confounded detective. I wish to Heaven I had sunk him at once! Not a moment's grace next time we meet, Mr. In- spector, not a moment!" "Good, Boss," said the Greaser. disguise shall I take?" The One-eyed Man thought a moment, and then said: "You must go from us as a sailor. and then proceed to Saffron Hill. Go to Luigi, hire a piano for the day, take it with you, play occasionally, and then go to Scot- land Yard. The organ will give enough local colour to your plan as a revengeful Italian. Luigi will find you a dress; he knows me. Now quit."

The Greaser looked at his chief in admira- tion. "Boss," he said, "there's brains in your belfry. Snakes! they are brains ! " "You will think there are brains at work, Greaser, when you hear the next plan. When the tide serves we will drop you down to the old rendezvous at Wapping, and land you to- night, and to-morrow morning you can go to Scotland Yard. Are you nervous of ventur- ing in the lion's den, Greaser?" The Greaser laughed. "Not I, Boss. I'd go to lunch with the Chief Commissioner, if he would have me in my rig-out." The next morning, about half-past eleven, a man attired as an organ-grinder ground out some weird tunes on a piano-organ in front of the entrance to Scotland Yard. A policeman on duty eyed him for a minute or two, and then said gruffly, "Move on." The organ-grinder smiled affably, and shewed a remarkably fine set of teeth in so doing. "r play ze fine tune, sare, ze opera, ze melody." The policeman grunted. said, "get off." But the Italian persisted. • "What place is zis? What place you call it? " The officer smiled, "It's a big police office," he said. "Now be off."
"Get off," he
"Police ofaz, good! The ver' place I want."
"You want?" echoed the policeman. "Yes, I want." "What do you want it for?" asked tho other.
"I tell sometings I know. Quick, let me in ze place. I not be seen outside here."
The officer looked at him with more than ordinary interest. "Wheel your organ in here." The Greaser did so. "Now," he. said, "what is it?"
The Greaser was not going to " split " there. It was to no ordinary policeman he was going to give his information. He wanted the inspector. "I see Boss," was all he would say. "I see Boss."

So, finally, after much argument, he was taken to a private room, and there' inter- viewed by the inspector in charge: But he was not to be drawn so easily. "I .want to see Mr. Bully, Inspector Bully." , The inspector thought for a moment. " Bully? " he queried. , "Bully? Are you sure of the name? Ah, by Jove! yes. .YOU niean Inspector Bullen. Yes, you can see him; he's in." The triumph of the Greaser was great, but his face was as emotionless as his com- patriots' plaster saints. . . . _

".Yas, Bullen, him I want, yes." ThV inspector in charqs rang a bell and a policeman entered. "Tell Inspector. Bullen he is wanted," he said. The policemen left the room, and in 'another minute Inspector Bullen entered. He nodded to the inspector in charge,„ saying, "What is it? "
:The inspector answered, "This Italian called to see you," and turning to the Greaser he said, "This is the officer you wished to see."

The Greaser pre a sweeping bow. "Sare, you once do good turn to me, and I repay you. Now, I gif you vol.' good information.'' Inspector Bul!en had done many good turns to people of all natio:!alities at odd times, and he nodded. "GO on."

The Greaser was volubility itself. " Sare,, you wish to ;MOW where Pali lif, the Austrian anarchist? yen, I know. I comes to tell you." He tapped his breast grandiloquently, after the manner of his race. " Sare, it is I, Pietro , Simini, ze pore organ-grinder know where Pori lif.7

; The inspector in charge opened his eves wide in blank surprise, and Inspector Buffett, scenting important information, put on his ; most businesslike air. Pari—Pari, the anar- chist— for \those arrest the Austrian Govern- ment offered a reward of ten thousand, kroner —roughly, one thousand pounds in English money! Here would be a capture indeed. i Addressing the Greaser, Inspector Bullen sakL "Your price? . There is a reward, you know."

The Grelser drew himseli* up with injured dignity. " Sare, I play ze melody, ze tune for money, and I play for ze lny of ze sunny land I leave—ze land ze melody brings back to my mind. But. sare, zis is honour—my honour —revenge to Pietib Simini, and I do not sell my honour. I touch not ze money." Inspector Bullen was interested. • A man does not forego mone'y for nothing, and a thousand pounds to an organ-grinder wluld have taken him hack to his beloved land a ' wealthy man. And yet he would not touch it. It must be a deep revenf;e, he thought, and more behind it, and he said so to the Greaser. !

The Greaser simply said: " Sare, it is blood money. I ..touch it not; my compatriot, Luigi, touch 'blood ,money. he die. I, no, sare. Again, sare, his comrades, Izi brothers, will ask NNW find who get ze money. Oh! -their arm it long; one month, two month, then it is kßowli Pietro Simini go back rich, who haf nothing,'

When he arrived back at the rendezvous and was once more closeted with the, One-eyed Man he related all that had happened. His chief warmly complimented him upon his cleverness, and regarding the diamond said: "Two thousand carats! Useless to me. Luigi is a fool. Why, the stone would have to he cut up to sell, and the cutting—well, anyone knows it's grass or, nettles cutting diamonds. No, Luigi, thank you, more work than break- ing in the Bank of -England to get it, and a white elephant when got. I have a finer scheme than that, Greaser, but it is not quite planned out yet. I want you •for another .errand now. Do you remember Bowery Kate'? Good you do. She is in London now, and has captured young 'Lord Armour. She is a soubrette at the Frivolity, under the name of' the Coney Island Coon. Her real name is Kate Martin. 'Made a hit with an insane song entitled 'l'll love you when your auburn whiskers grow'. That took with an equally insane public, and made her a favour- ite. This Lord Armour is badly hit. His father is the Earl of Elmore, owner of the famous Elmore rubies. Now, I have a market for rubies, but not for diamonds of two thou- sand carats. The son comes of age snext month, and Kate will be at the celebrations. The family seat is at Elmore Castle, on the Corn- ish coast. There is to be a great gathering of the clans, and if you. and I can get there, by Kate's help, the haul will be splendid. I merely suggest this as a sort of recreation, until my great scheme is matured. We must not rust, Greaser; there should be all of thirty thousand in it. Now, you must see Kate. She is staying in St. John's Wood— Shirley-road. Tell her the man who procured her father's escape from Sing Sing Gaol, New York, sent. you, and that she is to help you. You might go as a gentleman—it will be a change, eh?" The Greaser smiled. "We can play it though, Boss." "Yes. and to their cost," replied the One- eyed Man.

The next afternoon, a gentleman rang the rw-Al of 17, Shirley-road, and asked to see Miss Martin. After a few moments he Was admitted into a snug boudoir. Evidently, thought the man, "Bowery Kate" is tapping an insane public to some purpose, to judge by .the supe- rior appointments of the apartment.. Almost immediately the lady entered. She stared a moment at her visitor, then held out both hands effusively, saying: " Sakes ! If it ain't .Tames Wilton, and after all these years. Well, I'll be shot!" The Greaser smiled. He was waiting for that, for he had forgotten what the dickens his name was when he was introduced to her in New York. But, like a woman, She gave it away in her first burst of enthusiasm. "How's old Hiram? Is he going to walk right in?" " No," he said; "he's here in tondon. He asked me to call. Say, Kate, you're Instling things, oh?" and he pointed to the decora- tions. "Did you buy 'em?" She nodded. "Out of the great D.P.— two hundred pounds per week, four years' engagements. What do you think of that? How does it pan out with you, , are you doing bettor out of the London public?" "Say, how's the gilded jay bird—got him on the bird-lime yet?" .She nodded. "Fast as a church; we shall spliced soon, and then I break my con- tracts."

The Future of Labour.
The monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council was held in the Bold-street schools on Tuesday evening, Mr. T. Plumb presiding over a small attendance.

At the last meeting a deputation was appointed to wait upon the Ironworkers Society re the secession of that Society from the Trades Council. Mr. PLINSTON reported that he had not received a reply from the Society stating whether or not they were prepared to receive the deputation. The Executive Committee reported a joint meet- ing of the Committee and representatives of the War- rington Labour Representation Committee with refer- ence to the proposed unification of the labour forces of the town. Nothing was decided at the meeting. Mr. PLUMB said the Labour Representation Com- mittee delegates desired the Council to re-open the whole matter, and in face of what the Trades Council had done the Committee could not see their way to recommend the adoption of that course. Mr. SMITH pointed out that a ballot had been taken of the branches affiliated with the Trades Council. They could not go back upon the ballot.

Die SECRETAiiY reported that out of the 26 Branches affiliated with the Council 17 had replied in favour of the following question submitted to them "Are you in favour of the Trades Council remaining intact, with- drawing from the Warrington Labour Representation Committee aud making such alteration in the rules of the Council as will enable it to contest elections with trade union candidates only ?"

Mr. PLUMB said the Council had been a long time over the question of the unification of the labour forces but it was not-a question which they could play with and if they were to have a united labour force they would have to go about it very seriously. It seem to him that the decision arrived at was the only way in which the trade unionists of. Warrington would work at the present time. The failure of the Labour Repre- sentation Committee had proved sufficiently that the rank and file were not prepared to go in for an organiza- tion which admitted as members Socialist and Co- operative Societies. He thought the Council had acted wisely and it was necessary for them now to so alter their rules that they could take political action. They had been playing with the matter for some time and if they did not move more quickly than they had done they would have November upon them before they were prepared. To his mind they had nothing to hope for as Trade Unionist unless they took political action. They could sit there and discuss questions until doomsday but they would not do the slightest good unless they obtained direct representation. Councillor STOTT moved that the Executive Com- mittee be instructed to draft the new rules and submit them at the next meeting of tbe Council. He took it that they would at once withdraw from the Labour Representation Committee. Mr. MASSEY said they had been playing shuttlecock with the question for some time and it was time they came to the climax, seceded from the Labour Representation Committee and took action on their own.

Mr. HALEY said the vote showed that the affiliated Societies had not been satisfied with %hat bad been done by the Trades Council in the past, and be also accepted it as a distinct step forward in trade union work.

Mr. GREALEY moved that in the forming of the rules the extra expense entailed by the elections be met by a levy upon the membets. Mr. Slim! opposed this proposition and moved that the contribution he permanently increased. MI. GRUALEY thought Mr. Smith's suggestion would lead to extravagance.
Mr. PODMORE' : Extravagance can be avoided by the commonsense of the members of the Council.
The motion was approved

div.head: EXPLOITS OF THE OE-EYED MAN.
div.p: THE EXPLOITS OF THE OE-EYED MAN.
BY EDWARD TOWLER.
IV.-THE AFFAIR OF THE RUBY NECKLACE.

It was a bleak spot in the Essex marshes, ft spot as dismal and outlandish as one could well imagine. In the black, sluggish creek, surrounded by oozing banks of brown, wet mud, lay the Submarine, fitted with a new conning tower, and a flagstaff as brightly yellow as fifteen feet of new spruce fir could look. The flagstaff was not hoisted, for the reason that upon those flats even an object of only fifteen feet is seen from a considerable distance. A week had elapsed since Inspector Bullen had so miraculously escaped death at the hands of the One-eyed Man, and during that time the gang had lain quietly by in the backwaters of rivers and bays, doing nothing; simply letting matters rest, so as to strengthen the belief of Scotland Yard that the Sub- m-arine was no more.

When the shock of the collision had passed, Knd the One-eyed Man thought sufficient time had elapsed to allow the boat that had run them clown to disappear, they slowly rose to the surface. The hatch was raised, and when the One-eyed Man saw that both the tower and flagstaff had been torn away he cursed fluently. He was no fool; he knew the chances that a man had lashed to a spar, and he did not underrate the probability of the inspector being picked up. Whether he had been saved or not the One-eyed Man concluded that it would be safest to assume that he had, and to work accordingly. Therein lay the key to the extraordinary success of this man. He took nothing for granted. So, after a conference with the Greaser, the One-eyed Man said to him: •

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Ring of Spain's Palaces.—lt is common know ledge that Queen Victoria Eugenio has no liking for the Royal Palace at Madrid, where the little Prince of the Asturias was born last week, or for Madrid itself, which is certainly the least attractive town in Spain. The young Queen would much prefer El Pardo, which is situated at a short distance from the City, but conven- tion requires that at certain seasons, the King shall be in residence, in the capital, and the change,has not been practicable. The summer residence of the Spanish Court, at San Sebastiou, isperhaps of all King Alfonso's pal3ces, his Majesty's favourite. From the heights dominating San Bebastian—where lie the bones of the, English guards, who fell in the Peninsular wars—the most exquisite views crf sea-girt land, and snow-capped mountains, with the cobalt of sea and sky mingling on the horizon, can be obtained, and this particular panorama finds great favour with the Queen, whose childhood and girlhood were passed mainly at Osborne or in the highlands, and whose love tor the sea and mountains is well-known.

King Alfonso's Heir.—The flower of the pomeganate is the National floral emblem of Spain and this figures prominently in the layette of the little Prince, wel- corned *with so much enthusiasm by the Spanish people. It was on May 17th, twenty-one years ago, that the present King was born, a most important event for Spain, in view of the fact that he was a King from his first breath. Not quite so much depended upon the birth of the little Prince of the Asturias, but it has nevertheless been attended with all the pomp and circumstance that surrounds the birth of an heir to the Spanish throne. The little Prince has started his career of popularity under the happiest auguries, and he promises to become as great a favourite with the Spanish people, as is Queen Maud's little boy with the Norwegians. _ _ _

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—The Sunday Sch,,o Anniversary services in connection with the Wesleyan Church, attracted large congregations on Sunday, the preacher being the Rev. Geo. Llarbottle, of Matlock, a former minister of the circuit. Mr. Harbottle took for his text in the morning " Train ups child in the way he should go and when he.is old be will not depart from it," while in the evening his subject was He that overcometb shall inherit all things." A very pretty flower service was held in the afternoon nnder the presidency of Mr. El. W. Guest, of Warrington. The first lesson was recited by Miss Gertrude Page, and the second by Miss Minnie Dillaway, while two solos were rendered by the Misses Jessie Farrar and Lena Duck- worth. Miss Farrar also sang a solo in the evening,the chorus being taken up by the choir. Mr. Hugh Mellor presided at the organ,and praise is due to Mr. Johnson for the excellent manner in which he had trained the children for the afternoon service. The Submarine, with its collapsible rubber boat, lay off in the bay waiting for the rubieti that hung upon the neck of the Countess of Elmore.

During the evening the Countess was called away for a few moments, and was informed that a visitor wished to see her on very im- portant business. The visitor had been shewn into an ante-room, and, without the slightest suspicion of anything wrong, she entered the room. The moment she did so, she was seized and a chloroformed sponge was placed over her mouth, effectually preventing her from giving an alarm. Without a sound she became unconscious, and was placed in an easy-chair. The string of rubies was quickly unfastened from her neck and transferred to the pocket of the One-eyed Man, and a moment after he stepped out negligently, and joined the Greaser in the room where the dancing was in, progress..

"-Lei- us stroll out on the terrace," he said; "this room is confoundedly hot." The Greaser assented, and when outside he said to the One-eyed Man, "This job's a teaser. They are on her ladyship's neck, and will be transferred to the safe when she takes them off. How'll you get them, Boss?" "They are here," he said, tapping his breast pocket. "Let's quit. She's only enough chloroform for fifteen minutes, and it will take five to get to the boat." "Holy smoke!" ejaculated the Greaser. "Let's quit, by Heavens, right quick! What a man you are, Boss." „ . .

"Action is my motto, Greaser." he replied. "But come, quicken your pace." A minute more brought them to the boat, and in another five they ' were on .board the Submarine, which lay four hundred feet from the shore.
"We'll wait on deck, Greaser," said the One-eyed Man.

"Right," answered the other. - "There they go!" cried the One-eyed Man, as shouts reached their'ears, and many lights, flitting here and there, told of active search about the grounds. Then more cries, and, as the searchers neared the beach, the Greaser and the One-eyed Man stepped below, and the boat sank in forty feet of water, safe from ob- servation in the depths a the mighty ocean.

The agenda contained the following intimation : Following upon the close of each financial year impor- tant returns are made,involving considerable exceptional labour in the Clerk's department. The audit of Union accounts for the half-year ending at September, 1906, ended only on April 12th. Following upon completion of each audit are exceptional duties, and preceding each audit much preparatory work is also necessary—usually several months pass between each audit of accounts. The auditor, in response to enquiry by the clerk, stated he might audit accounts for the half-year ending at Lady. Day in July. His subsepient fixing of May 22nd, has required—with the unavoidable duties otherwise arising in each week—the whole time of the Clerk and his Staff to prepare for Audit, and will further require their attention until completion of the current quarter. The clerk in the interim will complete 35 years of service as Union Clerk, and Clerk of the Assessment Committee, and he will (unless it may prove more convenient, in the Union interests, to defer doing so, until the close of the current half-year) retire from the offices he has for so many years had the honour to fill. The Clerk will address a perfectly friendly letter thereon to the Chairman of the Board.

div.head: POWER FROM TIDES.
div.p: POWER FROM TIDES.

It has been estimated that the whole power of Niagara would not be sufficient to heat the offices and houses of a city as large as New York. From time to time suggestions have been made to utilise the energy of the tides, but the great difficulties of such a system are the small rise and fall of the tides in most situations, 'which, of course, means a low head, and also the intermittent nature of the flow of the tides. This latter drawback means that some special provision must be made for storing the power. The attention of inventors has also been turned to the problem of wave motors, but it must be confessed that any power .which we may be able to obtain from the ocean will be on such a small scale as to be almost negligible. Wind power is a more reliable source than waves or the tides. Solar radiation has also been a great attraction to the inventor. It is in districts where there is little rainfall, and where there is small chance of obtaining the energy of waterfalls, that there is usually plenty' of sunshine. If we work out the mechanical equivalent of solar radiation we find that it is nearly 10,000 h.p. per acre of surface exposed to the per- pendicular rays of the sun. But this figure applies only to certain latitudes, and however much this source of energy might be utilised, it would not, says Engineering Times, give us sufficient power to heat the great cities in cold climates.

div.head: PRIMITIVE MAN IN EGYPT.
div.p: PRIMITIVE MAN IN EGYPT.

A recent article in the. Scientific American calls attention to the results of excavations which have been carried on for some years in the neighbourhood of Naga-ed-Der, in Egypt, by Dr. J. C. Reisner. The site of the work is supposed to be that of the first settlement of man in Egypt, some 9,000 years ago. The region, now a desert, was then fer- tile, and had an abundant rainfall. Egypt did not then depend on the Nile for its fer- tility, A number of prehistoric mummies have been disinterred, preserved in salt, and wrapped in matting of halfa grass. These are specially interesting as indicating the first stages in the art of embalming which afterwards attained such perfection in Egypt. They seem also to, indicate that these primi- tive people held the belief that the

BODY WOULD Br. WANTED AGAIN. A careful examination of these well-pre- served skeletons reveals the important fact that the type has not changed in the long interval of 9,000 years. They are said to be racially identical with people now living in the country. The contents of the intestines are also preserved, shewing the food they ate and the medicine they took when they were sick. The diseases of which they died could also sometimes be diagnosed. Some had perished of kidney disease, others of gall-stones, or diseased bones. It is thus shewn that these diseases are not the result of modern civilisation.

div.head: QUARTZ GLASS MAKING.
div.p: QUARTZ GLASS MAKING.

Glass, so indispensable to the chemist and physicist as 'the material for experimental apparatus, has, nevertheless, its limitations. Chief among these, perhaps, says the Globe, is its fusibility at comparatively low tem- peratures. Hence it has been sought to sub- stitute for certain purposes vessels and other annaratus made of quartz. The advantages of this material are, that it can be heated to I,Boodeg. F. without softening, that its co- efficient of expansion is very small, that it can be heated red hot and plunged into cold water without cracking, and that it, permits the passage of the ultra-violet rays of light. But , quartz is one of the most

INTRACTABLE OF SUBSTANCES, and there are serious practical difficulties to overcome in utilising it for chemical and other apparatus. In Germany small vessels of a somewhat patchy nature have been made by beating small clear crystals of quartz and sticking them together, but there is a want of clearnosS in the resulting glass, oWing to the numerous air bubbles. It is claimed, however, that a considerable amount of sue- cess in making quartz glass has crowned the efforts of experimenters in the Carnegie Geophysical Laboratory, Washington. The great difficulty was to

GET RID OF THE BUBBLES, f and this has been achieved by " rst heating the quartz to a temperature of ,000 deg. F., and then, as it gradually • cools applying a pressure of 4001 b. or 500 lb. on the square inch. By this means a solid, clear quartz glass has been obtained. The bubbles are few and small, and do not interfere with the use of the glass in lenses and other optical instruments.

div.head: INCANDESCENT ILLUMINANTS.
div.p: INCANDESCENT ILLUMINANTS.

Mr. J. Swinburne, F.R.S., lecturing at the Royal Institution on this subject, pointed out that the incandescent mantle was now not only applied to the 'petroleum lamp, but to air carrying a little hydro-carbon gas, an ap- plication said to provide an extraordinarily cheap light. The facility to light by merely turning on had been achieved by the use of the bye-pass, and further advances were being made in this connection. Welsbach had discovered that an alloy of cerium and iron gave off sparks on being scraped or filed, and a burner had been designed in which the act of turning on the gas scraped a little wheel of this alloy, causing a spark which lighted the gas. Another invention permitted the gas to be LIGHTED FROM A MAIN TAP.

Each burner had an attachment which passed the gas straight through to the burner when the pressure was on; but, on turning the main supply off, and allowing a little gas to pass at the controlling tap, the attachment to each burner turned off the burner and lighted a little pilot jet which remained burning until light was again wanted. On turning on the main tap, the pilot jets lighted the various burners and were themselves extinguished. By this means burners could be fully lighted up by turning one tap at the door of any room. The electric incandescent light was undergoing great changes in the direction of the replacement of carbon by metal filaments. The

div.head: TANTALUM LAMP
div.p: TANTALUM LAMP

was now in great demand. It was made for 100 to 130 volts, and was much more efficient than the carbon lamp, although it did not last long on alternating current. The wires of a lamp that had been run for some time on direct current shewed a curious notch or crinkled appearance under the microscope. A wire that had been run on ail alt4rnating cir- cuit looked as if the metal had been :melted into short cylinders with round ends, and these cylinders had stuck together end to end without their centres being /in a line. Occa- sionally the little cylinders were nearly sepa- rated. This very extraordinary action had never been explained.• One of the most interesting of the new lamps was the

div.head: ZIRCON LAMP
div.p: ZIRCON LAMP

It was said to be made of zirconium and tung- sten, and lamps of this material had been made for 200 volts, which was of the greatest importance from the point of view Of distribu- tion. It was possible that the conductor was really a zirconide of tungsten, and, if so, this opened up a new series of compounds. A zir- con lamp for 100 volts had really six separate loops of wire mounted in series inside a: bulb. A recent improvement was to provide an ex- tremely light spring for each loop in order to keep it taut, and the lamp could then be used in any position. Tungsten seemed to be the favourite metal for new lamps, and it had the advantage of giving a very high efficiency. It was probable that the lamp of the future would have an efficiency of nearly one candle per watt; and this was promised by the use of tungsten. At the Came time it had to be ad- mitted that to make a wire .witn a resistance of 500 ohms small enough to give twenty candles with twenty watts would be a triumph of inventive skill.

div.p: REPORTS.

The report present bi—t-he--ACting Secretary (Mr. C. H. Dawson), stated that the programme given during last season included 32 ordinary performances and one mass performance. The Mayor in his speech after the latter spoke very highly of the music rendered in the Park by the bands. The financial statement showed that a balance of £l. 3s. 10d. was brought forward from last year. The contribution from the Corporation amounted to £7O and bank interest to is. 2d., making a total of £7l Os. Payments to bands amounted to £66 18s. 6d., leaving a balance of £4 10s. 6d. IS MUSICAL ENTHUSIASM DECLINING? _

The Ciiaiß-.4-a-isr -OC;;;;;;tie-cr upon the satisfactory character of last year's work and expressed the hope that the Association had a prosperous season before it. Since they met last year two musicians well-known to them all had been ,removed by death. He alluded to Mr. William Cummins and Mr. Thos. George Grounds. Both had done excellent work in the cause of music and they would be much missed. He felt that at the present time there was not the enthusiasm in musical affairs in Warrington that there was a' few years ago. Many of thtir best bandsmen were getting on in years and they could not expect them to always have the energy for playing instruments that they had now ; and yet young players did not seem to be springing up in the necessary numbers to fill their places. He did not think young men as a rule now took the study of musical instru. ments seriously enough. Other pursuits doubtless interfered with musical study more than formerly, but as his late father once remarked at an annual meeting of the Association, "the time will come *hen the inclination for active pursuits will no longer be felt, and then will be the time when the true value of the study of music in youth will be appreciated." Perhaps it was this cause which made the older men usually more enthusiastic than the younger ones. He thought it was a matter for serious consideration byall instrumentalists as to whether they were putting all the enthusiasm they could into their own musical work and whether they were by example and by encouragement doing all that was to possible induce young men to take up and seriously, study so me musical instrument with the fixed determin- ation to become expert players, not necessarily for pro- fessional purposes but for their own enjoyment and for the enjoyment of others.Mr.Down concluded by eulogis- ing the services rendere4 to the Association during the last eight years by Mr. Wadsworth who, he said, was elected secretary in January 1899 on the retirement of Mr. Taylor. The way in which he had conducted the affairs of the Association deserved their highest praise. It had been decided that they ought to express their thanks not in mere words but in a more practical manner, so he had great pleasure in calling upon Mr. Thomas Armstrong to offer to Mr. Wadsworth a small token of their regard and appreciation. (Applause.)

div.head: PRESONTION TO MR. WADSViTORTH.
div.p: PRESONTION TO MR. WADSViTORTH.

Mr. THOMAS ARMSTRONG then handed a beautiful gold alhert to Mr. Wadsworth, expressing the hope that he would long be spared to wear it and that it would always remind him of the Association of Bands. (Applause.) Mr. WADSWORTH, who had a very cordial reception, said he could hardly find words to express how ex- tremely pleased he was to receive their valuable present, and his appreciation of the goodwill which had prompted it. It was also very gratifying to see such a large attendance of bandsmen, for he felt sure that many of them had come to see the presentation. They need not make him any present to make him remember Warrington. He came to the town a stripling from college, without any experience and for some years served as a teacher at People's College. His connection with the bandsmen of Warrington had enabled him to know something of their self-sacrifice and to appreciate them work. He believed they occasionally felt, as they had expressed it at meetings of the Association, that as far as payment was concerned, their services were not valued suffi- ciently highly, but they must, at any rate, know that the general public appreciated their work, as was proved by the large attendances at the Park. Such demonstrations as those on Lifeboat Saturday and Hospital Saturday could scarcely succeed but for the readiness and ability of the bands, and he begged the bandsmen, if ever they were invited to assist on such occasions, to refuse, as they had done before, to let any misunderstandings or neglect interfere with the harmony of the proceedings. Their performances probably did more for the people of Warringron and district than they were aware of. He considered that during the past six or eight years Warrington had made progress in musical matters. (Hear, hear.) Three or four bands had been formed in that time—Crosfleld's, Walker's, Legh-street (re-organised), and League Junior Band, he believed—and he had also been pleased to notice an improvement in the programmes and in the playing. Mr. Armstrong must have covered acres of manuscript in writing music for the btnds. (Laughter and applause). Then, they had two excellent male voice choirs in War- rington—probably the only town in the kingdom of its size with two such large and highly trained bodies of men singers, able to hold their own against and even defeat ail-corners at competitions. Two or three chil- dren's choirs existed in the town, and were a credit to it. The church and chapel choirs were also doing an excellent work, and there were several vocal quartette parties who were able to interpret the beat music. Mr. Wadsworth alluded to Sir Edward Elgar's declaration that the musical centre of England was not London, but the Lancashire district, and expressed the hope that that reputation would be maintained. He urged the bandsmen to aim at greater perfection, and then they might one day have the pleasure of seeing a Warrington band carry off the first prize at Belle Vue. (Applause). The CHAIRMAN referred to the tactful way in which Mr. Wadsworth discharged the secretarial duties, and moved a vote of thanks to him for his energetic and enthusiastic services. It was due to him to a very great extent that the Association was as firmly established as it was.
Mr. SMITH seconded, and the vote was very heartily accorded.
ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The following officers were elected :—President, Mr. Arthur Down; vice-presidents, the 'Mayor (Alderman Smethurst), Mr. 01. Monks, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., Mr. R. A. Naylor, and the members of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee; hon. treasurer, Mr. John Fairhurst; hon. sec., Mr. C. H. Dawson.

div.head: -A St G GBSTION.
div.p: -A St G GBSTION.

It was suggested that the male- voice choire might give perforn ances in the Park, but it was pointed out that there was a great difficulty in giving effective vocal performances in the band stand. Votes of thanks to the Mayor for the use of the Council Chamber, to the police, Town Hall, Perks and Baths Committee, the Press and officials were accorded, and the meeting closed with a similar compliment to the Chairman.

WOMEN LIP.ERALS AND THE PREMIER. I TIE) Women's Liberal Federation strongly complained ! on Wednesday that the Women's Qiialineation Bill had , been sent to the House of Lords. The Prime Minister ; sent a reply on Thursday stating that that was done to save time, in order to secure the passage of the Bill through both Houses. Sir Henry added that he did not think it necessary for him to receive a deputation on the subject. The delegates considered the reply satis- factory, and loudly cheered the reading of the letter.

div.head: VOTES FOR WOMEN. --- '— Meeting in Support at Warrington.
div.p: VOTES FOR WOMEN. --- '— Meeting in Support at Warrington.
The cause of women's suffrage was advocated at a

public meetidg held on Tuesday afternoon in Toft's Assembly room. There was a good attendance, Miss Massy presiding. The principal speakers were Mrs. Alan Bright, of Liverpool, and Miss Lucy Broadbent, warden of the Church Hostel, Manchester. A letter of apology for non-attendance was received from Mrs. C. E. Parker.

Mrs. BRIGHT in a highly interesting address referred to her experiences in the Wimbledon election, pointing out that people of all shades of opinion, Liberals, Con- servatives and Labour, had rallied to support the ' suffragist candidate, all animated by a desire to advance a just and right cause. The time was bound to come when this cause would meet with fulfilment. Several arguments had been adduced against women's suffrage. The only argument that was brought forward at all persistently was that women did not want the vote. There was a certain amount of truth in that, but the fact that leisured people did not want, it did not count for much. Mr. Chaplin at Wimbledon issued a placard bearing the words" No thank you, my dear, you must stay at home and mind the baby. That was a good deal spoilt by the fact that at the same time,Mr. Chaplin, who had already 200 ladies working for him, was urgently asking for more lady workers to canvas for him. He did not explain who was to mind the babies of those 200 ladies. (Laughter). Leisured women, perhaps, did not want the vote, but working women engaged in public work, teachers and factory hands did want it. The whole condition of life had changed in recent years. The occupations of women to-day in certain fields of labour were threatened, and it was a hard thing for women to know that the Acts which governed factories might be altered more or less at the instigation of men land without women having any influence whatever in those regulations. She claimed there was justice in the women's claim that they urgently needed the vote to safeguard their rights and possibilities of work. She I also claimed that women in public offices, women as guardians, district or parish councillors, as teachers and inspectors women in every form of public life needed not only the rights they had to-day safegagrding, but insuring to them for the future. The influence of woman was a pretty thing and to a certain extent was useful, but unless it *as backed bp by the power of the vote it was like a frail reed or a staff of painted paper which when they wanted support would crumble and break in their bands. It was suggested at Wimbledon that if women had votes there might be discord at home. That was disproved by the success which had attended the franchise extended to women in New Zealand and Australia. Those women had had their interest in public affairs stirred. No party had particularly benefitted by increased votes as the result of the franchise extended to women. Therefore, she thought they might safely look upon the future development of the franchise in this country as as a thing that would make for the good of the whole community, and not for the breaking up of home life. As the struggle for life increased every day there must come a time when there would be a great tepdency among men to crush women out of the work they had to do. They wanted women to have votes so that they would not run the risk of being crushed out. How were they going to get the vote? There was only one way and that was by enlisting the spmpathy of their men friends. If they could only convince the men of the justice of their cause then the cause was half won. (Applause). I ADDRESS BY MISS LUCY BROADBENT.

Miss LUCY BROADBENT said she was.present to plead the cause of women's suffrage, as a Conservative, for she believed that the enfranchisement of women was a measure entirely in accordance with the spirit of the English constitution. The principle of no taxation 'without representation was one of the bulwarks of their constitution. They asked therefore, for nothing strange or revolutionary, but.simply for that elementary justice to which every British subject was entitled. But more than that, they were only seeking to restore to woman the rights which she once possessed. It was not till the Reform Bill of 1832 that the Parlia- mentary franchise was limited to men, though ever since the seventeenth century the tide had been turn- ing. And what was the result of the limiting of woman's power? In the eighteenth century, when they bad practically no education, and were relegated solely to domestic duties, public morality was at its lowest and corruption everywhere rife. What e contrast to the sixteenth century, when they received what we should describe as the higher edccation, and when they were intimately associated with politics ! The six- teenth century, whatever its faults, was a century of great causes and great men. And now, when under another women's rule, the education ideal of the 16th century had been realized, when not only the upper classes, but every woman had a chance of receiving a good education, could they justly be debarred from exercising those rights which were open to the most ignorant of men? What a pity that the Parliamentary vote could not be made to depend on a certain standard of intelligence instead of being determined by the sex of the voter. (Hear, hear, and applause.) It was perhaps well to debate some of the objections that were raised. She had never heard any logical objection. There was only a mass of sentiment and prejudice but that, as John Stuart Mill observed, was more difficult to treat. There was a letter in the "Spectator "about a fortnight ago in which the writer said that women by their action in this matter were forcing men to assert the foundation fact of nature, i.e., the supremacy of the masculine sex in all final issues. Apparently he based that supremacy on the fact that men were physically stronger therefore. that might was right. But the whole tendency of civilization in its upward progress was a protest against that doctrine. Might was not right except among savages. Reason, law and justice they believed to be right. She would contend as earnestly as anyone for the domestic duties of a woman. She questioned whether they did not cripple her in the performance of these duties, and lower her conception of their grandeur, when they did not teach her to regard herself as a citizen. Some objectors said, rather inconsequently, that the possession of the suffrage would make women irreligious. To increase their duties as citizens, so to work that Christ should not have such terrible cause to weep over their cities as He wept over Jerusalem, was to ensure that their faith should find its due expression in action. An objection frequently raised was that the franchise would distract woman from her duties in the home. Those who said that forgot that an election onlyltook place about every five years, and the busiest woman could spare one hour in five years without serious detriment to the childran's dinners. ( Applause).l Legislation every year became more and more far reaching, and dealt with questions which concerned women very intimately. Were women to have no voice in the education of children, in the alteration of the! marriage laws, in the management of factories and shops where women worked, in the regulations for domestic servants? If they lived in an ideal society there might be some reason for not desiring a change, but let them open their eyes. Look at the overcrowdipg, not only in London, but in every large town. There were hundreds of women who could not live a decent life for that cause alone. Look at the multudes of public-houses. Look at the sweating system. She had seen women in East London wearing out heart and brain in making boxes for twopence an hour. "If only you women cared," said Ruskin," you could prevent it." Ah, yes, if they cared, but they did not care. That was the pity of it and the shame. They shut their eyes and refused to see. But here were these crying evils, which men had failed to cure. Should they not, therefore, work heart and soul to secure their rightful place in the community. that they might help to redress thsse bitter wrongs? (Applause). Miss SYLVIA BROADBENT asked Mrs. Bright if she did not think women's suffrage,would make the country much more democratic. At present the Government of the country was largely in the hands of thelmeducated 'classes. It was not good to be governed by those who had not the time and ability to think of important I subjects, and if more power was to be given to the uneducated classes the country would become tuore democratic—which she thought would be an unfortun- ate thing, as the franchise was tie) large already. Work- ing men who knocked about the world generally had a better chance of judging what was right than women lin the same station of life. She felt that the franchise would be enormous and unweildy if all the women had it.

Mrs. ItonEwr GanNErr asked would the franchise give equal yaws to women as to men. She understood it was for spinsters and widows only. Mrs. BRIGHT, in replying, said Miss Sylvia Broad- bent had raised a curious point. One of the great objections the Labour Party had to the members of the National Union of Women barrage Societies was that they were pushing forward a Bill for the enfranchise- ment of women exactly on the same terms as men, and that they were therefore going to add enormously to the property vote. As a matter-of-fact Miss Broadbent was right and the Labour Party were wrong, because the percentage of women who would be enfranchised under any Bill which would give the vote to women on the same terms as to the men would enfranchise a larger proportion of working women. But she was afraid her very large experience of canvassing did not enable her to agree with Miss Broadbent, as :he found that the average factory woman sr working woman was as well educated as the average working men. She agreed with Miss Lucy Broadbent that there should be an education test for the franchise and nine out of every ten women would pass it. She thought the time had not yet come for manhood suffrage. It would be much better for the country and the welfare of all classes if, instead of accepting man- hood suffrage, they had a measure enfranchising women and so level up the classes all round. _ _ _

The Rev. J. P. AIATTHEWS thought the whole question I ought to be, submitted for public discussion. He was not sure whether the contention lay between the moderate Bill now before Parliament aid adult suffrage. He fancied the true position of the Labour Party was tha.t they objected to the present Bill because they would much rather see a Bill for the introduction of universal suffrage making woman the absolute equal of , man in matters which had to do with Government. He I combatted the idea that only educated people were capable of taking an interest in public questions.Wonrn as women deserved the suffrage, but be did not think they would get any sympathy from a Tory Government or the present Liberal Government. The inherent I prejudice of men towards women in this matter had to be attacked and broken down.

T'ne brief statement made THE ETHICS OF by Mr. WINSTON CHURCHILL
JOURNALISM. on Wednesday in reply

to a question from Mr., LEHMANN is one of the most plainspoken things that can have been said in either H mse of Parlia- ment since the begiCling of Parliamentary insti- tutions. It charges a certain newspaper, which we have certainly no disposition to name, with the invention of a story. With this class of • newspaper everything is "a story," or rather nothing is of importance unless it is " a story." It charges this class of newspaper we repeat, with bastless and impuleat fabrica- tion in regard to a matter which deeply concerns Imperial relationships. Wh tt W 33 related, said Mr. CHURCHILL, bare not the slighte3t resemblance to anything that took place at the Imperial Con- ference. This has been c mroboratel by the Premier of Newfoundland in an interview. Mr. CHURCHILL added that it was a matter of surprise to him that a person receatly cre dad a peer should permit the newspapers which he owns to pursue methods "of such transparent mendacity.,' Tile subject thus dealt with in the House of Commons is not one that we should have. been disposed to raise on our own acount. If we had made Mr. CHURCHILL'S complaint, in howsoever mild a form, it would probably have been consid- erered by a large number of our readers that it was merely a case of one newspap-r making an attack upon another, as a little E4tanswill affair, in fact. Mr. CHURCHILL has placed the matter in its right relations. He has lifted it out of the region of difference of opinion or of conduct between one newspaper and another into the region of Imperial politics. Here, as he clearly indicates, is a case in which "transparent men- dacity " is employed to prejudice the relations between Great Britain and one of her Oolonies. We have grown much accustomed to transparent mendacity from the same source, and we do not call into question the right of a newspaper to lie if it supposes lying to be good business, but here again Mr. CHURCHILL hits the right nail on the head. The proprietor of the newspaper in question has recently been raised to the House of Lords. That position must be supposed to involve certain rather serious responsibilities. There is also involved a rather grave question. Was he raised to that position because he was expected by that party, to which he owed his pro- motion, to serve it in the manner which was so frankly and vigorously and truthfully characterised by INlr.CuunculLL on Wednesday ?A. country with a free choice as to its newspapers, gets, of course, the newspaper that it deserves. The general question, which might also be considered a personal question, is one into which we do not propose to enter.
