div.p: An attempt has been made to teach us that American methods of journalism are "the thing." It has to be replied first of all that American methods of journalism are exceedingly various,and that the best are English. No American journalist has up to this time succeeded ;on: the:English Press, and many English journalists have succeeded .013 the better side of the American Press. These statements are indisputable. But the 'characteristic of the baser part of the Amer-- Can Press is to disdain accuracy and to tell 'a story." This sort of thing is being introduced into England under the influence of immense Wealth and with lamentable effect. It is the Instinct of the Englishman to believe what he reads in the newspapers. It has been a true Instinct in the times past, because the first instruc- tlen to every English journalist has been to be accurate. To make that instruction read aslan Instruction, to invent a lie nag, we believe, received .a severe and, we hope, a crushing blow from Mr. WINSTON CHURCHILL.

Not much has been heard of WARRINGTON late with reference to the LAY-BYE. proposed increased utiliza- tion of the lay-bye on the Is• SulP Canal at Walton. It is evident, however, that local commercial concerns are interesting themselves in the scheme, for in the year book of -ttl,le Manchester, Liverpool and District Tanners' -ederation just issued, Mr. W. B. Moston in an article on the Manchester Ship Canal says:— Warrington lay-bye is not yet in active use as a calling place for the various foreign and coasting earners, but it is hoped that the energetic efforts %We in this direction will soon have the desired Teault. The Canal Company have completed some I,alprovements at this lay-bye to facilitate the 4,andling of traffic, and during the past year have 'auted a commodious warehouse for storage." We ;;clially re-echo the hope expressed by Mr. 4toBton that the lay-bye will soon be taken full Ildvantage of, for we are confident that the project oee fraught with great possibilities to the nl 'omercial prosperity of Warrington.

It will be fresh in the GARDEN SUBURBS. memories of our readers that a Garden Suburbs '"heme for Warrington was successfully inaugur- ated some months ago. We hear that the project is being most enthusiastically taken up, the pro- ,raoters having an admirable site at Great Sankey le view, and there is every indication that the 'efforts which are being put forth by those who are anxious to secure model dwellings amidst health- ful for the working classes, will be eeowned with success. The Garden City move- Inent has proved a welcome innovation in other Parts. of the country and the system of the Po-partnership Tenants Housing Council which is • active operation atEaling should do a great deal In the direction of solving the housing problem. ir John Brunner, Bart., M.P., the president, has c°,n,cieelY stated the aims of this organisation. icles new suburb," he says, "too often repeats the faults of the old town, and possibilities of 131;a0e, fresh air and sunshine, gardens and common • aYgrounds have been shortsightedly thrown a'waY• The object of the Co-partnership Tenants' li „ "sing Council is to prevent the repetition and f:.rPetuation of this mistake, and to take what my teed Mr. Vivian rightly calls the long view, not re short view, in the development of building ae• Its methods are sound and practical ; they eels the merits of the economy which wholesale as,Ving in land effects, they have all the merits of shi‘enlatic development which municipal owner- le: ef houses secures, and, at the same time, th owner- ewe of its risks; and furthermore, they enlist ,wka.t interest and responsibility of the individual vt„."101 are so entirely necessary for complete success" e are glad to hear that the movement is making pid strides, notably at }tiling, and the fact that 1: Possesses such influential and enervetic helpers Sir J T. Brunner and Mr. Henry Vivian, M.P., sufficient guarantee of the sound business Principles on which it is conducted. Warrington "ahould not be behind the times in this important enterprise, and we hope that when the proposal is Placed before the public it will be sympathetically 'received and substantially supported.

"Music in the Park" has MUSIC IN THE become so firmly established PARK. among the popular forms of outdoor enjoyment during ,the summer months, that the public perhaps the realise the extent of their todebtedness to .‘,./ae members of the local bands who occupy the ",and so frequently. Too much praise cannot be Riv!he to the Association of Bands which caters for enjoyment of the townspeople in this way and ."8 gratifying to find that the Association is in a e-ltisfactory position and numbers many musical iethusiasts within its ranks. At the annual meet- On Monday opportunity was taken to fittingly nize the services of Mr. B. Wadsworth who and etly relinquished the secretaryship after long devoted services. He thoroughly deserved t. le tangible tribute to his work, for the Associa- Ti°e owes much to his unremitting exertions. Vteresting speeches were delivered by the , 2esident (Mr. Arthur Down) and Mr. Wads- who both touched upon points of great 'llterest to the musical life of our town. Mr. Down rightly made a plea for greater interest in the I9,2ric of bands and we hope his appeal to young "13 in particular to devote themselves to serious Musical study will not be in vain. Mr. Wadsworth been attention to the advancement which has made of late years in Warrington's musical affairs and pointed with pride to the existence of '3znellent male voice choirs, bands and other 2tßanizations which have maJe very gratifying I;eaclway. There has certainly been a musical revival in Warringt-m, and that it may be main- tained will be the sincere wish of all who take an ..Mterest in the culture and innocent recreation of townspeole.
Now that the Colonial Con- THE COLONIAL ference has concluded, the CONFERENCE. Premiers who have taken

part in it as the representa- tl'es of distant parts of the Empire are permitting d "ernselves some freedom in referring to its pro- e_.,edings. Mr. Deakin and Dr. J ameson, the chief rocates of Colonial Preference, have explained that they, at any rate, are disappointed at the I:Psuit of the meetings. The Premier of the Cape declares that one thing only has been accom- Thished—the alteration of the name from Colonial " to " Imperial " Conference. That, however, is not so small a change as might appear °ll the surface. In his address in opening the Ineetings, Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman insisted 'l2l the character of the gathering as a Confer- ice not between the British Government and the subject States, but between the Government Of the Mother Country and the Governments 'l4 the Sister States on equal terms. That was I,ll',Stel) forward from the old conception of the ~ i„""ations between the delegates; and the alteration the name which gratifies Dr. Jameson so —uco was the natural outcome of the ,lttitude taken up by the British Premier. el:he development of the 'usefulness of the Confer- :cc' is a matter of time. This year many days .oere spent in discussing the practicability of °lonia' Preference, and from the point of view of WOrk accomplished that must be regarded as so 'lOl time wasted. Neither Dr. Jameson nor Mr. tr, skin can really have expected the Government accept their proposals. The General Election of ths4 Year precluded them from doing so, for abl4 question of Free Trade was unquestion- tb the foremost issue in that contest. So ,(13 st the disappointment which they express b ust have been somewhat discounted before- I ca'lud by the knowledge that they were pleading a pens°, upon which for a few years, at any rate, the es,c)rue of England had made up their minds by e:ablishing the Liberal Party in power. That, of souu_lB. e, does not prevent the Colonies, if they are weupposed, from carrying on what Missionary r„K they desire. If they can convert the electors i'neir view, with the help of Tariff Reformers

here, well and good. But because in this matter the Government have taken the full significanc4 of their mandate is no reason to suggest that th Conference itself has been a failure. As a matter of fact, there has been substantial gain in the position of the Mother Country and the Colonies towards each other.
One remark made by Lord THE EX-SOLDIER'S Lansdowne at the meeting CLAIM, of the Society for Employ

ment of Reserve and Dim charged Soldiers well deserves attention. Why is it that the ex-sailor. has no difficulty in getting employment while the ex-soldier is often reduced to penury, and sometimes has to beg in the streets, making a pitiful show of his ribbons ? The 1 number of war medals that came into the market soon after their distribution for services in the South Africa War was a melancholy evidence of the condition to which some of the bravest men in the country were reduced. The answer,broadly speaking, to Lord Lansdowne's question is that the sailoc.is recognised, both in prose and verse, as a " hal4dy-man," and the belief is that, even though he may not be up to a trade, he will soon learn it. His life on board a vessel is supposed to make him resourceful, though, prabably, his ability is quite as much due to travel and observation. But the soldier ought to be able to get work without makieg any excessive demand on our patriotism. He should be secured by care in training him, if possible, in one or another branch of industry—even for a short time —while he is engaged in his military training. It would not, surely, lessen the inclination to enlist- ment if a raw recruit were to know that he would be made more efficient, not only for military, but also for civil life when his military term was over. Mr. Haldane is understood to be anxious to do something for the soldier in this respect. And if an ex-soldier be capable, there can surely be no two opinions about the propriety of giving him preferenoe when one considers that he offers his life for his country, and in a percentage of cases risks his health in the duty.

What is believed to be a record attendance at school has been made at Richmond, where Jessie Illobday has attended every school day without once being late, from the age of three to fourteen. This makes eleren years' perfect attendance, and she has won every award the Education Committee can offer. She has a silver medal for seven years' attendance, a silver watch, and several other valuable prizes. o _ _

Our readers will be interested .to hear that Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., had the privilege of dining with the Prime Minister at 10, Downing-street, some ten days ago. On Wednesday evening Mr. Crosfield and Miss Crosfield gave a dinner party at Hyde Park Hotel to a number of friends in honour of the Prime Minister and other members of the Government and the Liberal party. * * *

An exceptionally attractive prograurne has been arranged for the Warrington Volunteer Prize meeting which takes place at Appleton to-day (Saturday) and on Monday. The chief trophies to be competed for are the battalion shield presented by Colonel MacCarthy O'Leary for the company with the highest figure of merit in 1907 and the silver bowl presented by General F. Roome, C. 8., for the company with the second highest figure of merit in 1907. * *

Warrington's popular Mayor had an exceedingly busy day yesterday when he visited the various elementary schools to encourage the children in their Empire Day celebrations and to present the medals and brooches which the Mayoress and himself gener- ously gave to the scholars selected for this honour by the votes of their fellow-pupils. His Worship made the round in a motor car and at each school delivered an address full of good advice.

* * * The widening of Bridge-street and Market-Gate is again occupying the practical attention of the Corpor- ation and this week workmen have been engaged in demolishing the few remaining shops in Bridge-street. It is undarstood that the Corporation is now seriously contemplating the commencing of operations in Buttermarket-street, so that it would appear that Alderman Bennett's dream of the Warrington of the future, as relates to the centre of the town, is ou a way to realization. ** * _ _

T'was the last straw which broke the camel's back. For some considerable time the Warrington Trades and Labour Council has held its meetings in the Bold- street schools. Recently they have been greatly inconvenienced by the prepartions for the great Wesleyan Bazaar and at their April meeting they could not, so to speak, hear their own ears on account of the indefatigable efforts of certain bandsmen who were practising most enthusiastically in an adjoining room. The delegates revolted and now the fresh quarters are being sought. * * Our readers will be glad to hear that his Majesty the King has been pleased to signify his desire to personally congratulate Mr. John Kirk upon the com- pletion of his forty years' work for the Ragged School Union, and will receive him at Buckingham Palace at 11 o'clock on Thursday, May 23rd. It will be remem- bered that only a fortnight ago Mr. Kirk visited Warrington to take part in the celebration of the twentieth anniversary of the Ragged School. His addresses on that occasion deeply impressed his hearers, and showed how thoroughly earnest he is in his efforts to uplift the slum children, and give them a fair chance in life. * * *

Thursday was an important anniversary in the Liberal calendar, for it was on May 16th that no less I than three members of the Cabinet first saw the light. Sir Henry Fowler—who with the exception of Lord Ripon, is the oldest member of the Government celebrated his sbventy-seventh birthday. Next in seniority comes Earl Carrington, President of the Board of Agriculture,who was sixty-fonr on Thnrsday. The last and youngest of the trio is Lord Elgin, Secretary for the -Colonies. His Lordship, it is interesting to note, is of Colonial birth, having been born at Montreal fifty-eight years ago, when his father was Governor-General of the Dominion—a post also filled by his grandfather. * * * A Scotch clergyman is accustomed to use scientific terms which the people do not understand. A deputa- tion waited on him recently with the request that in future whenever he used such terms he would explain them. On the following Sunday he used the term, hyperbole, and added, As agreed on I beg to ex- plain this word. Were Ito say that at this moment the whole of my congregation are sound asleep it would be hyperbole, but if I say that one-half are asleep that is no hyperbole, but the truth." The next day the deputation again called to say that then minister need not explain technical terms. The people would learn their meaning from a dictionary. —" The Tatler."

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, May 18,1907
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 18,1907

The report was presented at a meeting of delegates held in Preston on Saturday, and remarked: "Towards the overthrow of a Government false to its pledges, unscrupulous and tyrannical in action, devoid of con- structive statesmanship, and totally oblivious to the true Imperial interests of the empire, let your efforts be directed. By so doing let the fatal folly of the last election be expurgated, and the hasty verdict given in a moment of passionate unretlection annulled." The work of the Government is reviewed, and, of course, condemned; there is not a single redeeming feature. The report almost equals in bitterness the last one presented at a meeting held in Warrington. The overwhelming defeat of 1906 still rankles, and the Federation has taken it in anything but a sportman- like spirit. ,
- Good sense and good nature are never separated.— DRYDEN. _ _
Do not mind being insulted, but be very careful not to insult. —EmEnsos.

hours' day for train workers and a ten hours' day for the other grades. During the past twenty years a great change had come over railway work. In those days a very heavy load for an engine was about thirty full waggons, but now engines were so powerful that they could drag from sixty to seventy full waggons. The result of this was that fewer men were employed. During the past two or three years there had been a decrease of 10,000 in the number of railway workers, in spite of the fact that the amount of railway traffic had gone up by leaps and bounds. They knew that although the number of men had been decreased the wages of the men had not been increased [accordingly. This was something which they wanted to bring about, and for that purpose he urged all grades of railway men to combine. There were men going up and down the country preaching that the Government had not done anything for the workers of the country, but during the last session the Government, through the influence of the Labour party, had done more for the workers than had been done in the previous ten years.—Mr. W. Fl. Maybury proposed a resolution approving of the pro- gramme drafted by their delegates at Birmingham. Councillor James Sexton, of the Dockers' Union, sup- ported, and said that the national all-grades movement was a great step, but he thought the idea should be enlarge& and the railway workers should join hands with all the sections of the transport trade. That would be a most effective step in placing the workers in position to obtain fair treatment. The safety and interest of the publit demanded that the railways of the country should be national property. If that was done, then they would have a far better chance by legislation in reducing the hours and increasing the pay of the railway workers.—Councillor Hammond (Blackburn) and Councillor Forshaw (St. Helens) also supported, and the resolution carried.

div.head: WARRINGTON
div.p: WARRINGTON
Coming Events. Warrington's annual horse parade will take place on Saturday next. Full details will be published next week. _ _ _

• Thursday will witness a welcome revival of the Lymm May Queen festival, which will be attended by the old-time dances and the customary revels on the green. As in the past the preliminary procession will cr nstitute a special and most attractive feature and in this connection valuable prizes are offered for the best decorated vehicles,- cycles, &c. By the kindness of the Rector the children taking part will be entertained to tea in the schools. Altogether the pageant promises to be as gorgeous as any of past yearn and will doubtless attract thousands of sightseers to the village.

On Friday eveninr, week a meeting in support of the Bishop of Liverpool's Fund, will be held in the Co-operative Hall. The Mayor will preside and addresses will be delivered by the Bishop, the Rev. Canon Willis, Mr. J. D. Buckton and others. "LEA-FRANCIS," "PREMIER," and " BUDGE- WHITWORTH " CYCLES. Price from 10s. Cash or easy payments.--J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. District Nursing Association. The Workingmen's Committee of this Association acknowledge with thanks the receipt of £l2 12s. from the Warrington Football Club. Corporation Appointments. The appointments of Mr. Martin Nicholls as chief constable and Mr. J. Coote Hibbert, as medical officer of health were unanimously confirmed by the General Purposes Committee yesterday. The infirmary and Dispensary. The Hon. Treasurer to the Workingmen's Com- mittee begs to acknowledge with thanks, the sum of 21, received from the Warrington Football Club, being a portion of the gate receipts taken at the recent Works Competition matches.

The eighteenth annual show of the Warrington and District Agricultural Society will be held in Welton Park on Thursday, 14th August. Prizes, cups, &e„ are offered to the value of about 750. There are classes for shires, hunters, hackneys, harness horses, jumpers, tradesmen's or tenant farmers, txrnouts, cattle, pigs, cheese and butter. Entry forms and all particulars may be obtained from Mr. H. Beresford Melville, Bold-street, Warrington. Entries close on Wednesday, 31st July. The Lawson Contraet. An action was recently commenced in the High Court against the Warrington Corporation by Mr George Lawson to recover £36,000 alleged to be due in respect of the waterworks contract. The Town Clerk took out a summons to dismiss the action on the ground that plaintiff was bound to go to arbitra- tion. The Court has appointed as arbitrator (by mutual consent) Mr. George Hill, C.E , who holds the position of consulting engineer to the Manchester Corporation. Warrington Whitsuntide attractions this year, in the way of entertainment, will consist of an excellent display of animated pictures in the Parr Hall. This is being promoted by the Imperial Animated Picture Co., who on Monday open a fortnight's visit here. The performances are being run on the two shows a night principle, and commence at 7 and 9 o'clock. At each an excellent and varied programme of animated pictures will be presented, these including humorous, pathetic and informing pictures of a high order. Picture songs will also be given by the Lynches, and altogether an admirable entertainment is promised. - - • •

Warrington Technical Building Students' Association. , -

The members of the above association on Saturday ; afternoon paid a visit to Messrs. Crosfield's New Cement Works, Bank Quay, now approaching corn- pletion, the visit being the practical side of the sub- ' , ject of Dr. Prentice's lecture on Portland cement at the Technical Institute a few weeks ago. The students were met by Dr. Prentice, Mr. Newall and , Mr. Wilson. They first had the pleasant but some- what exciting experience of ascending and crossing the new transporter bridge to arrive at the works. Here Dr. Prentice explained the process carried out by the various machines. Owing to the bow nature of the ground great difficulty had been experienced inl , obtaining the foundations to carry the massive con- crete columns and heavy machinery for the manu- facture of cement. This however, has been overcome lby an original and ingenious idea of concrete Piles. IThe mode of making and fixing them to a depth of 130 to 40 feet in the ground as explained by Mr. Newall and Mr. Wilson was at once interesting to members lof such an association. Considerable interest was also taken in the method of wood piling to the jetty !alongside the works. After a little discussion on the ; properties and the mode of mixing concrete the party I was rowed across the river, then taken through the soap works to the dining hall where an excellent tea was provided and needless to say thoroughly appreci- ated. A hearty vote of thanks to Messrs. Crosfield's ' and the gentlemen who had so willingly conducted the students over the works brought an interesting and instructive visit to a close.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
WIDNES MANHOOD.

At Widnes, on Monday, before Major Wareing (in'the chair), and Alderman S. Quinn, Michael Donelan (60), residing at 42, Charlotte-street, was charged with unlaw- fully wounding his wife by striking her on the head with a ring gasburner. On Saturday evening she stated that she went ont,leaving her husband in the house, drunk. Returning at 10.15 by the back door, she found the house in darkness, and after lighting the gas, exclaimed what is home without a mother." Prisoner got hold of a plate to strike her, but was prevented. She rushed to the front door, which was locked. Prisoner followed her, and threw a ring burner at her, causing two large lacerated wounds on the head, penetrating to the bone. Dr. Eustace described the wounds, and said that he feared complications. A remand until Thursday was granted.—Joseph M'Mahon, Caroline-street, was charged and remanded until Thursday on a charge of wounding his mother, Ann Brodigan, by stabbing her in the eye with a table knife. Prisoner came home late on Sunday and was remonstrated with by his mother. He picked up a knife and said he would "stick her." He struck at her body, but the knife did not penetrate her clothing. After Wards he struck her on the eye, the blade cutting the eye just above the pupil. Dr. Eustace stated that he might save the eye, although he wound was serious.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday, when there were present :—Messrs. T. Baxter (presiding), J. Spruce, S. Woodward, T. Wright, J. B. Chadwick, C. E. Linaker, P. Booth, P. Collins, A. Haining, J. Alynekyme, J. Hallows, C. Rnylance, C. F. Bell, W. M. Morris, T. Guest, P. Mounfield, H. Mawdsley, A. Broome. J. Ren- shaw, W. Harrison, G. Pilling, E. Bretherton, E. Britch, J. L. .ones, G. Egerton Warburton, J. H. Davies, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk), T. Cook, W. R. de Prez. and J. Pearson (relieving officers), and J. Cunnah (master.) The Clerk intimated that Mr. Charles H. Hoult, Egypt-street, Warrington, had beea appointed assistant overseer for Grappenhall, at a salary of £4O per annum. The appointment was confirmed without comment. The Clerk read a letter from the National Anti- Vaccination League asking the Board to instruct the vaccination officer to take such proceedings against parents who declined to have their children vaccinated as would necessitate only one attendance at Court and render possible a reduction of the maximum penalty now imposed on the second appearance for disobedience of the magistrates, order. The letter was allowed to lie on the table. The Finance Committee reported payment in out- relief of £2O to Mr. Cook, £32 to Mr. de Prez, and £24 to Mr. Pearson.

RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there were present : Messrs. G. Piling, T. Baxter, J. Spruce, S. Woodward, T. Wright, J. B. Chadwick, C. E. Linaker, P. Booth, A. Haining, Mynekvme, J. Hallows, C. Roylance. C. F. Bell, T. 'Guest, P. Mown. field, H. Mawdsley. A. Broome, J. Renshaw, W. Harrison, G. Pilling, E. Bretherton' E. Britch, J. L. Jones, G. Egerton Warburton, J. H. Davies G. F. Ashton (clerk), W.E. Hough (assistant clerk),J. Davies, and W. Digglo (surveyors), J. Farrington (inspector), and Dr. Adams (medical officer). ' The Clerk read a letter from the Office of Woods stating that Lord Carrington desired to know whether there was any demand in the district for allotments or small holdings. He would be glad if there was a genuine demand to endeavour to arrange, if it could be done without undue disturbance to existing tenants,to utilize portions of the Crown lands in the district of the Council that were suitable for the purpose of allotments and small holdings. The Council's co-operation in the matter would be appreciated. Mr. Harrison said they could not expect applications for allotments until the terms of the holding were know. Mr. Woodward said he had had one genuine applica- tion from a suitable person for a small holding. He did not see that much could be done in the matter until the details and conditions of the allotments were before the authority.. They could not deal with the question until they knew the terms. Mr. Linaker asked if the Commissioner of Woods would send circulars to be distributed asking for applications for allotments, and the applicants also to state whether they desired the whole of the capital to be provided for the erection of buildings. They would then be able to ascertain if there was really any desire for small holdings. As to rent, &c., that would of course depend upon the quality ol the land. He moved that the Clerk ask the Commissioner of Woods for circulars inviting applications. This motion was approved. The Clerk read the followina letter from Mr. J. E. Sacker (Messrs John White and Co., Warrington) : The dust nuisance at Daresbury is becoming most serious.' I wrote to Mr. Linnell and enclose a copy of his reply. Does the Rural District Council purpose doing any- thing? Personally I think the offer of the County Council was rather one-sided—in their favour. If they had provided the calcium I could have undertaken to spread it. Would you mention the matter to your Council and ask for urgency in the matter. The letter referred to by Mr. Seeker was :—Wit regard to the dust if the inhabitants or local authority will find the dust-layer either calcium, chloride or westrumite the Council will put it on. The former costs 30s. a ton ad it will take five, tons to dress the road twice over and rather less for subsequent dressings. We do not allow oil on the road. Mr. Woodward moved that the application be not entertained. He did not think they should deal with any County roads for which they had no responsibility They had sufficient to do without spending money on the County roads, and if they wanted to experiment they should do soon their own roads.

The motion was approved. The clerk intimated the receipt of a writ from the Runcorn Urban District Council. The plaintiffs claim for an injunction to restrain the District Council from connecting a sewer with sewers the property of the Urban District Council. Mr. Woodward: Is it not a fact that this sewer belongs to the Manchester Ship Canal Company. The clerk: That is the contention of the Manchester Ship Canal Company. The clerk intimated that he had, instructed his agents to appear in answer to the writ. The action of the clerk was confirmed. The clerk reported that Dr. Selby had inspectel the new mortuary and said it did not answer requirements in any particular. There was no provision at all for conducting post-mortem examinations. The Norley Water Commtttee recommended that only that portion of the scheme be carried out (at a cost of about £300,) which relates to the distriot in and near Blakemore-lane, which will supply about 26 houses. Mr. Woodward said the Committee were not prepared to spend the money required for, the larger scheme. He moved the adoption of the scheme. Mr. Bell moved the postponement of the scheme until the Parish Coancil had had the opportunity to prove that the wells and springs in the district could be improved, and the supply rendered fit and adequate. Mr. Roylance moved as a further amendment that the whole scheme be proceeded with. It was not reasonable to supply one portion of Norley at the expense of the other portions of the parish. Water was badly wanted in Norley. _ _ . . _ _

_ Mr. Linaker said that with refarence to Mr. Bell, he would point out that the question had been before the District Council for years, and that the owners of the property in Norley had promised time after time to repair the wells and springs, but had not done so. The small scheme wauld cost Norley id. in the 2, whilst the larger scheme would cost about 10d. in the 2. The recommendation was approved.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
RAILWAYATEN'S HEFTING AT ST. HELENS.

Mr. T. 'Mover, the local M.P., presided at a great meeting of railway men held at St. Helens Town Hall on Sunday, in support of the national " all-grades " movement of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants.—Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P. for Newton, wrote expressing sympathy with their demand, and regretting his inability to be present.—The Chairman said that was likely to be for ever regarded as a red-letter day for the railway workers of the country. One of the objects of that meeting was to induce all non-members to join the society, and they wanted all the workers of the country to give a decision on the position of affairs. They must that day show whether or not they were anxious to have their wishes further pressed on the railway companies. The correspendence which had been read showed that all the companies were united in denying to their men the right to be repre- sented by the beads of their organisations. He claimed that the demands of the railway men were perfectly fair and reasonable. It was not a case of isolated action in this matter. The men were acting unitedly, and all grades of the workers were eombining in the movement. The men were asking for an eight

div.head: ST. HELENS MOTHER.
div.p: A ST. HELENS MOTHER.

Margaret Stevens, married woman, was charged, at St. Helens on Monday, with neglecting her two children. 'An.. E. W. Swift said that Inspector Luff removed the woman's two children to the wol khouse. They were in a neglected condition, and were stunted and diseased through neglect. The woman had for a long time been under the supervision of the officer of the N.S.P.C.C. but she gave way to drink. Her husband on this occasion called in the officer. The prisoner's husband now came forward and pleaded for leniency. Mr. Swift said that everything else had been tried, and he thought the only remedy remaining was a period of imprisonment.—The magistrates sent Mrs. Stevens to gaol for a month's hard labour.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

THEFT FROM A SHOP DO9RWAY. At Newton Petty Sessions, George Watts, a small boy, was charged with stealing a jacket and vest from the doorway of Mr. Jones, pawnbroker, Market-street, Earlestown. He admitted the offence.—William Hughes, assistant at 27, Market-street, identified the jacket and vest produced, which he missed from the doorway about noon on May lst.—A lad named Thomas Morris, living at 42, Market-street, said he saw Watts take the things from the doorway, and gave information at the shop.— P.C. Lennie deposed to finding the prisoner at a house in Tamworth-street. Before that he had made enquiries and found the lad's parents living in Chapman-street, Gorton. The boy's father gave up the things to witness. The family had lived in Earlestown till about a year ago, and the home surroundings were bad.—The Bench ordered prisoner to have 13 strokes with a birch rod,and then to be handed over to the Gorton police, who, it was stated, wanted him for a similar offence there.
VIADUCT INSTITUTE TECHNICAL: INSTRUCTION CLASSES.

The presentation of prizes and certificates to the successful competitors in the various examinations held in March, April, and May, 190 took place last Thursday at the Institute. There were on the platform Messrs. H. D. Earl, J.P. in the chair), R. Brocklebank (a director of the L. and N.-W. Railway Co.), C. B. F. Borron, W. Thompson, W. Collingwood, A. Smith, T. Ormand (secretary), J. H. Graham (class secretary), &c. —Mr. Earl referred to the very good work done in the classes under very disadvantageous circumstances owing to the classes being held in different parts of the town instead of being in one building. Plans had been passed by the Board of Education and County Council, and the money necessary to build the new Technical School was applied for. That would be a great impetus to education in the district. The number of students registered ten years ago was 467 • last session it was 1,142. The number examined had risen from 205 to 429, and those successful from 187 to 263. The subjects taught were now 25 as compared with 17, and the grant obtained was £213 IGs., as against £96 7s. 6d.--Mr. Brocklebank said education must always be in two forms—literary and technical. The combination here was excellent. They had the Works, and in the Institute they taught the literary part. The necessity for educa- tion was always increasing—one could learn, however old one grew. Still, they must have a foundation, and it was a foundation they desired to give in that Insti- tute, to help in forming character. This country was suffering from being an old country more than anything else. For a long time we had been living on our reputation, but we found that although our reputation was still the best in the world we lad to meet American and German competition, while, just at the present moment, the Japanese also were spreading themselves all over the world. In tho management of these ,:vorks and institu- tions there must be two classes of people— workmen and administrators. The responsibilities of those who managed were heavy in many cases, and the responsibilities of the workmen were heavy in their way. What they wanted in institutes of that kind was to work together, with the same object in view ; and, if they did that, they would have the best possible results.—During the evening a very enjoyable musical programme was submitted by Mr. Harry Collins and party, all the items being keenly appreciated. Mr. Collins, besides being a humorist, gave evidence of talent in a musical direction. Miss Alice Collins, Miss Clara Collier, and Mr. W. H. Atkinson were the vocalists, their singing being of a high order.

div.head: ST. BARNABAS' SALE OF FUND. Church E)—&—niion Work.
div.p: ST. BARNABAS' SALE OF FUND. Church E)—&—niion Work.

- The Church extension fund was again the ,object in aid of which the annual sale of work in connection with St. Barnabas' Churrh was held in the Assembly Room at the Conservative Club on Wednesday and Thursday. The room had been brightly decorated, and there was a good display of useful and fancy goods. The following presided at the stalls : Toy Stall.—Miss Fry, Miss A. Fry, Miss I. Johnson, Miss IC. Cole. Work Stall, No. I.—Mrs. Liddall, ' s Bolton, Mrs. McDowell, Mrs. Head. Young Alen's Bible Class.—Mr. W. Turner ( ary), assisted by members of the class and the fo owing ladies: Miss A. Jones, Miss Evans and Miss Elsie Evans. China Stall.—Mrs. Allen. Work stall No. 2.—Mrs. Evans, Mrs. Randalls, Mrs. , Glassbrook. 1 Young Women's Bible Class.—Mrs. J. H. G. Holling- worth, assisted by memberEc of the class. Work Stall, No. 3.—Mrs. Gregory, Mrs. Birchall, Mrs. Shaw. . Refreshment Stall.—Mrs. Connell, Miss S. White- house, Miss E. Whitehouse, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. W. Jones, Mrs. Grounds, Mrs. Greenhalgb, Mrs. Proud. Flower Stall.—Miss A. Whitehouse, Mrs. Hands. The sale was opened on Wednesday afternoon by Mrs. J. D. Buckton. The VICAR (Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth) having apologised for the absence of Lady Greenall, who forwarded a cheque for £25, and Mr. W. A. Proud (people's warden), who was detained in London, said he was very grateful for the efforts of the workers of the parish who had helped to prepare for the sale. The response to their appeal had been liberal and most of the goods had been contributed by parishioners. There had been the utmost unanimity and good feelingamongs the workers this year and he thought that was a sign of progress in the right direction. He knew from other clergymen's experiences that there was seldom a sale of work without some needless friction and annoyance. That spirit had been entirely absent this year. As to the church extension fund to which the proceeds would be devoted, they wanted a chancel, side aisles and an organ. The fund was progressing slowly but surely,and they hoped soon to have sufficient money to build an organ if it were possible without enlarging the chancel. Perhaps some well-to-do millionaire might help them in that effort—at any rate there would be no harm in making application. They were fortunate in having obtained the help of Mrs. Buckton, who was well kNown for the keen interest she took in Church matters. (Applause). Mrs. BIICKTON said she felt great sympathy with the outlying parishes of Warrington which were not before the public in the same manner as the larger and dlder parishes from which they had been carved. She knew that the clergymen who had charge of them, and their , wives and parish helpers did a great deal and worked nobly. Therefore she thought they deserved as much help as could be given to them and she wished that , effort every success. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr. ALLEN a vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Buckton and the sale commenced. The sale was re-opened on Thursday afternoon by Miss White, Holly House. The VCAR announced that the proceeds for Wednes- day amounted to £7735. Miss WRITE said she was glad to be present on that - interesting occasion. She remembered the laying of the foundation stone and the consecration of St. Barnabas' Church with the growing population and the erection of new houses the extension of the church was very necessary. A vote of thanks was accorded to Miss White on the proposition of the Vicar. Miss Turner's anartette party was in attendance each day and played selections. The total proceeds of the sale amounted to £125 is. 4d.

div.head: VOICE OF LABOUR.
div.p: THE VOICE OF LABOUR.

Edited by John Workman. Readers of this column are invited to assist in making it interesting and helpful to social workers by contributing th,eniselves. Correspcnulents must write on one side of the paper only, and endeavour to make their letters and notes short and to the point. A nom-de-plume may be used, but the real name of the writer should be forwarded in confidence to the Editor of the column. M.S.S. must be addressed to John Workman, " Examiner " Office, Warringtom and should be sent in not later than Wednesday in each week.

-- This week there is much to be saidfor Socialism The views expressed in this column, little as they may be held by some, have not yet received that criticism which one was led to expect. It may be, of course, that up to now the various arguments have been unanswerable. This week there is something for the opponents of Socialism to think about. I have had the pleasure of listening to the very able addresses recently delivered at Bridge Foot by Mr. T. Russell Williams,the Socialist candidate for Hudders- field. He is a cultured speaker —one of the finest in the movement. His straightforward and intelli- gent definitions of Socialism are worth repeat- ing here so that those who are able may try their best and hardest to refute them. Socialism," says Mr. Williams, "is the recognition of the law of our social being. It is the principle of State interference carried to its logical conclusion, under democratic auspices. It is the application of the principle to politics that an things that are Socially needed ought to be Socially owned." ' Some time ago the president of the Warrington Liberal Association argued that "a nyin should get his produce, his whole produce, and nothing but his produce." That means, I think, !" Every man for himself and perdition take the hind- most." lam inclined to believe that that is selfish- ness and, the Rev. R. J. Campbell says, selfishness is

I understand that the branches affiliated to the Trades Council have practically unanimously decided to recede from the Warrington Labour Representation Committee, and enter into politics "on their own " by putting forward trades union candidates for local elections.
Perhaps " The Scout" will give us his views in the matter next week.
POLITICS.

On Sunday 'Morning Mr. Williams spoke on current politics, and said that the difference between the Liberal and Tory parties was that which existed between Bill Sykes and Pagan. He severely con- demned the action of the Liberal party in bringing the Army Reform Bill before Parliament. He said it was only paving the way to conscription. The pro- posal to give a preference in connection with Civil Service appointments to men who had served behind the colours was a pernicious one and ought to be resisted by all men interested in peace and the welfare of civil

Referring to the Finance Bill, Mr. Williams said that at Huddersfield Mr. Winston Churchill said the Liberal party was going to give old age pensions to the working classes. The promise had saved Huddersfield for Liberalism at the bye-election. Mr. Churchill had also said that if 10s. a week were given to the aged poor it would mean an annual expenditure of £120,000,000." I don't agree with the figures" said the speaker"but I am not concerned to challenge them." As a matter of fact they only serve to emphasise the ridiculousness of the Liberal proposals; for if 10s. requires an expenditure of £120,000,000 a year, how much can you get from a million and a half ?" (Laughter.) Mr. Asquith's proposal amounted to a pension of 11d. a week That would buy half-an-ounce of thick twist every Saturday morning. Mr Williams then spoke of a prominent Yorkshire Liberal who had become so disgusted with his party's action in this patter that he had resigned.' SOCIALISM AND INDIVIDUAL MORALITY.

In the evening Mr. Williams took for his subject "Socialism and Individual Morality." The lecturer began by admitting the need for individual strife after holiness, • but contended that rich and poor :alike were handi- capped by the artificial restrictions of the present Competitive System. .ie illustrated hlw the practice of attempting to undersell each other in the open market cramped the souls of business men, and made the poor dishonest. The greed of gain, he declared, was engendered by the fear of poverty. The great hindrance to reform was the way in which the strong were allowed to victimise the weak, and the crafty were able to gain an advantage over the honourable. He laid great emphasis on the need for recognising the law of our social life ; and pointed out that it was by means of the principle of State interference that evil men had been compelled tY recognise their brother's rights. Socialism sought to extend the principle by means of gradual process. " The institute of industrial freedom," said the speaker "would elevate the morals of the people and place the life of the nation on a higher plane."

div.head: DRINK TRAFFIC.
div.p: THE DRINK TRAFFIC.

On Monday night Mr. Williams' lectured on "The Drink Traffic." He argued in favour of public management, but admitted the need for a policy of individual reclamation. He urged his hearers not to believe that the I.L.P. was opposed to remperance Reform and declared that very few I.L.P. clubs had anything to do with the sale of intoxicants. The reason they got int ) cinflict with the Temperance party sometimes was because Temperance Reformers were accustomed to say that poverty was chiefly caused by drunkenness. That was not true. Drunkenness aggravated poverty, but in very few cases was drunken- ness the sole cause of poverty. The Tuesday night's meeting had to be abandoned because of the rain. It was disappointing. Mr. Williams ought to be invited to speak in the Parr Hall, and His Worship the Mayor ought to take , the chair. He is a public benefactor. MAN, TUE WEA.LTII-MAKER. I wrote last week, Mr. Editor, that our means of Wealth-making had sadly outstripped our methods of Wealth Distribution, and when we consider the magnificent control mankind has • obtained over the I productive forces and powers of nature we stand amazed at the unconquerable spirit of man, which by toil, genius and skill cipapels the earth to give of her varied treasure in overflowing abundance. Our shops and warehouses, our ships, docks, factories and works testify to the success of man's efforts to win that which he seeds. We know there is no shortage in necessary, useful and even ornamental things. Thi4 is so, not- withstanding that many members of society are sheer idlers, parasites, non-producers. The economic period, at the end of which we stand and from which eventu- ally a new social order will CO9lO, is marked by the organisation of production and exchange of wealth. The competitive age we are passing through—the struggle for prizes —has promoted the use and development of natural gifts, and has created wonderful machinery for productions and splendid facilities for market and exchange. The knowledge and experience gained in the long combative years have ' become the property of Society, and cannot be taken away. Let no man say there is not enough and to spare for all. Nature's home of plenty is full to overflowing of all necessary good for the physical basis of human life. The problem is not wealth-production—this is already solved, its possibility and sufficiency proved beyond all cavil. But wealth distribution on a just human basis remains to be achieved. We who march in the ranks of labour, manual and intellectual alike ask of mankind to devote itself to this problem with the same energy, thought and skill that have been too exclusively and for far too long spent on wealth making. Access to the means of wealth, pro- duction for use and consumption, the freest facilities for the development of our best, the common needs of our common humanity to be asserted and satisfied— these are what we ask for, and in asking we have our faces to the light, like him who wrote Let dead hearts tarry and trade and marry, And trembling, nurse their dreams of mirth, While we the living our lives are giving To bring the bright new world to birth. LAZARUS.

ARE SOCIALISTS FOOLS? 1 The hydrocephalic hobbledehogs who write the leading articles for the" Gutter Press !" unhesitatingly answer the above question in the affirmative. To them, Socialism is a scheme of contradictions, illogicalities and absurdities, promulgated by fools or knaves, and attracting to its ranks only the ignorant and foolish. As these infantile wiseacres are seldom right we should have no need to bother with their statements were it not for the fact that the constant reiteration, the parrot-like repetition of a statement often leads people to believe at last that there must be. some truth in it. So it is with the scribesof the " Daily Pail." Without understanding they have preached the folly of Socialism until many people may have come to believe
that Socialism really is an organized folly and that Socialists are fools.

Now Socialism means the substitution of collective enterprise, the transference of the Land and Capital of the country from private ownership to public ownership, and the organization of industry for the benefit of the community. For instance, Warrington owns its Tramways, its Gas and Waterworks, makes electricity and in several other directions Manifests its Municipal Activities. The result is —better services ' than would be provided by private enterprise, lower cost of the various commodities supplied, fairer wages and conditions for the labour employed and—a profit in relief of the rates. Socialists urge with irrefra,ga,ble logic, that if it is wise for Warrington to supply its own gas it would be wise also to supply its own coal. If water, why not bread? If electricity, why not many other things which are just as essential to modern life? Reduced to plain English, the folly of Socialists lies in the fact that in an age of muddy thinking, their reasoning is clear, their logic is sound, their folly is the folly of wisdom. Just suppose far a moment that Warrington was so delighted with its present municipal ventures and their success that it had applied for and obtained permission to municipalize the local "Driek. Trade," what would happen? The quality of drink supplied would be of the best, the inducements to ex-eessive indulgence would be removed, and a large revenue would be obtained every year which would probably suffice ter raze all the slums and build in their stead healthy and beautiful dwellings, in a few years making "Beautiful Warrington" a fact and not as now an empty or ironical phrase. That is the sort of thing Socialists aim at and they know it can only be obtained by the extension of municipal and national enterprise. If this be folly who would be wise?

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

• Cricket. Orford Barracks at the present moment have the honour of heading the Warrington and District Cricket League, having won both the matches which they have played. On Saturday they entertained the" Guardian" eleven,and running up 74,0ut of which B.Day knocked up- 28,they dismissed the Printers for 50,Gleason and Knight working havoc amongst the stumps. The effectiveness. of both men can be judged by the fact that in every case they hit the wickets. Wilderspool Brewery and Bewsey Wesleyans had a fairly close fight, from which the Wilderspool.men emerged victorious by ten runs. C.L.C. Engineers accounted for Walker's Brewery rather by their bowling and fielding than by wielding the willow. Castle Rubber came a cropper, and in response to a total of 46 by St. James' ceuld only run up twelve.

-- In the first division of the South-West Lancashire League, Stanley defeated Newton, and St. Helene proved too strong for Earlestown. St. Helens Recs.,on the other hand, after a very closegight with Prescot.lost by the narrowest possible margin, scoring 116 to 117 by their opponents.

Playing for Penketh, Ward was in splendid form and criptured seven West Derby wickets for eight runs. So effective was his bowling that West Derby could only reach a total of 15 in reply to a total of 41 by Penketh.

The outstanding feature of the game between Avenue Juniors and Warrington Excelsiors was the batting of Jolley and LAwton. For the winners Jolley scored 32 out of 80, whilst Lawton notched 29 out of the 70 runs placed to the credit of Excelsior.
Monks, Hall 2nd had to thank Llewellyn for their defeat on Saturday by Latchford Baptist 2nd, as eisbt of their men who fell before his deliveries could between them only secure six runs.
ja --

Sankey Wire Mills 2nri met and defeated St. Paul's the respective totals being 42 and 23. For the winners Hewitt batted well for 19 whilst none of the defeated eleven succeeded in reaching double figures.

Batting against Moore and Dareshury Latchford Baptist ran up 45 and then prepared to take a turn at leather bunting. They however had little of this to do as eight flyers finished the match, Conway and Clifle dismissing the men from the country for 11 Conway in partilular was in fine form and bagged G. wickets for 4 runs.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

The Warrington clubs represented in the seninr com- petition of the Lancashire and Cheshire County Bowling Asrociation. have both succeeded in surviving the first rouad, and judging by the form shown the probability is that the progress of neither will be seriously checked until thA later stages in the tournament. Playing at Leigh it Lily( ay the Cemetery team accounted for the Prestwich representatives by 201 points to 182. The surprise of the match was the failure of T. Bolton who could only secure five marks to his opponents 21. The left handed trundler has evidently not yet found his form but in this he is not alone as his captain amongst others also failed to do himself justice. Bulls Head made even lighter of the task set them in the opening round and very easily accounted for Harpurbey. All the men were in fine trim and even those who were unfor- tunate enough to be beaten suffered defeat by narrow margins only.

If the Warrington Works Association can continue to provide fare throughout the season equal to that of the first two days they will prosper exceedingly from the point of view of the number of spectators witnessing the matches. The opening day's play saw a match pulled out of the lire in the last minute, and won by the smallest possible of margins, and history repeated itself on Saturday when Locker's and Fletcher's (No. 2) tried conclusions. If the expression is permissible Locker's set off with great ecl at, and A. Ford in ten ends gave his side a lead of fourteen points. Fletcher's responded gallantly, and turning the tables on Crozier, Hitchmough brought the teams within five points of each other. A succession of wins placed Locker's in a strong position, and they were not in the least disconcerted when R. Roberts dropped a point especially as W. Roberts retrieved the position, and with seven men off the green increased his team's lead to one of 10 points.

Fletcher's were not feeling over happy, but Atherton placed a little heart into his men by winning 15-8. Another victory to Locker's followed, awl then, so to speak,the fun began. Davies in the first half of his game had a stiff fight with NLather, and at the twelfth end the two men were level. Then bavies found his length and nal home before his opponent could again secure the block. Saunders made matters more interesting by winning 15-6, and with one game undecided Locker's led by three points. Both teams watched therr representa- tives closely, and Pletcher's were in high feather when they saw Rigby having matters all his own way. They required fourteen points to win, and when Rigby led 12-4 they regarded the game as settled. Ashton, how- ever, began to assert himself, and *ten he ran from 13-6 to 13 all the Palatine players were not a little anxious, and their depression was increased when Locker's man went to the front. Then to their great joy Rigby good another wood I-ome. It mattered little that Ashton won the game, as Rigby had secured the necessary points, and Fletcher's had qualified for the second round.

Penketh and Rylauds (No. 3) also had a close fight. Like Locker's, Ryland's opened well but could not keep up the pace and with six men off the green a lead of 17 had been lost and they were one p Ant in arrears. They regained the lead but Penketh forged ahead, and ere the close of the game had secured the verdict by ten points despite the fact that their last three representatives had to admit defeat. Whitecross (No. 2) made but a poor show against C.L.C. and from start to finish were behind, the railway men winning by 53 points.

To-day's matches are : London and North-Western Railway v. Pearson and Knowles. Robinson's v. Rylaud's No. 1. Walker's Brewery v. Artingstall's. Referee, W. Simister. Matches for Saturday, May 25th. Rylands' No. 2 v. Monks. Hall No. 1. Fletcher's No. 1 v. Crosfield's No. 1. Castle Rubber Co. v. Thewlis and Griffiths. Referee, G. Ball.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

St. John's Presbyterian Church. On Sunday the anniversary services were held at St. John's when the Rev. Dr. A. de Vlieger, of Chorlton- cum-dardy, preached morning and evening. There were good attendances at each service, especially in the evening when Dr. de Vlieger preached from the text" I am the true vine' and my father is the husband- man," John, xv., 1. Dr. de Vlieger said that as they knew from the passage in the fifth chapter of Isaiah, the figure of the vine as applied to the Church of God was well known to the Jews. Among the branches of the vine there were those that might be called merely nominal and those that were real. It was not flattering to them that they were told that there were on the vine of -which the Father was the husbandman, some branches which could never bear fruit, and which were, therefore, not essential branches of the vine. As the branch was united to the vine so they must be united to Christ. Jesus said" Abide in Me and I will abide in you." As long as they were united to Christ there could 13) fruit. Special hymns were sung and at the evening service the choir gave a rendering of the anthem "Seek ye the Lord," the solo part being taken by Miss Adams. Mr. J. W. Jowett, church organist at St. John's, presided at the organ. Satisfactory collections were obtained at each service. Wycliffe P.S.A. Annual Meeting.

The annual meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. was held ton Sunday, the Rev. John Yonge presiding over a large attendance. Certain formal business having been transacted, the meeting proceeded with the election of officers, which resulted as follows :—President, Rev. j. Yonge ; treasurer, Mr. R. Atkinson; secTetary, Mr. B. Farrar; assistant secretary, Mr. W. Farrar; registration secretaries, Mr. W. Rutter and Mr. J. E. Hewitt; absentee secretary, Mr. R. Mills; benevolent secretary and treasurer, Mr. J. Owen; markers, Messrs. W. and H. Farrar; stewards, Messrs. T. Wood, E. Smith. W. Sparkes, J. Dutton, J. Ford and H. Taker; committee. Messrs. W. H. Payton, W. Beswick, J. Bailey, C. Cross- kill, J. Ratcliffe, A. Healey. G. Wallington, G. Smiley, .T. Simcock. .1. Garner. G. Colley, C. Cotton, J. R. Palmer, J. Gresty, T. Ellison, D. McEachern, R,. Lewis, 3. H. Archer, and S. Massey. The balance sheet, which was adopted, showed that the total income of the Society had been £159 14s. Bd. and the expenditure £l7l 17s. 7d., £5O having been handed over to the fund for the renovation of the Wycliffe organ. The committee in their 14th annual report had to regret that there had not been an increase in the membership of the Society or in the average attend- ance. Whatever the cause they must hope that they had reached the low water mark and from that day they must all seek to be active workers in connection with the brotherhood. Instead of 500 their membership should be 1006—(hear. hear)—and whilst the slight decrease in numbers which had to be recorded was dis- appointing it might be the means of filling all with a determination to work and bring about a better state of things. Their membership at the close of the year was 507 or 36 less than during the preceding twelve months and the average attendance was 320 each Sun- day. During the year the prizes awarded to the mem- bers numbered 623 or 113 less than in 1905 and'brnught the total since the formation of the Society to 12,055. Sympathetic reference was made to the loss which the Society had sustained by the death of several members. The Secretary of the benevolent fund, continued the report, had been able to meet all claims and the same applied to the secretary of the sick fund which was steadily doing its work although heavily drawn upon at the latter end of the year. The savings club also con- tinued an important branch of their operations. Their meetings during the year had all been of a high tone and the aims of the Society had been kept well to the f ront.The visitation work was again heartily commended and an appeal was made to the members to interest them- selves in this work. The importance of energetic visita- tion had been shown in Halifax where the membership of a Society had been raised by this means from 500 to 1000. The work of the various officers was highly praised and the report concluded by urging the members to renew their activities and to work hard for the cause of the brotherhood so that at the close of the coming year they would be able to say that it had been the happiest and most successful in their history, and that they had reached a membership of 1000.

The huge success of the Works Competition resulted in a disposable balance of nearly £lO3 after payment of expenses. Grants have been made to injured players &c., amounting to £9 10s. ; Infirmary Extension, £5O; Infirmary Revenue Fund, 20 guineas; Nurses' Institu- tion, 12 guineas; and the St. John's Ambulance, £6. Through our heavy casualty season 1905-6, the Insur- ance Society again increased the premium, and lam sorry that owing to so many claims again this season that they have made no gain. div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
A SUCCESSFUL SEASON.
The report and statement of accounts on the past year's work of the Warrington Football Club have been issued this week. .•
The SECRETARY (Mr. H. Ashton) reports as follows :

The first team have played 43 matches, won 29, lost 13 and drawn 1. Much concern was manifest at the commencement of the season through the dri stic changes in the rules pro- viding 13 aside,instead of 15, play the ball and a penalty for touch-kicking. Such ;iterations had a very import- ant bearing on the game abd much anxiety existed in the minds of the legislators of the Northern Union as to their success. Our players by assiduous practice,and with the help and judioous coaching of our local referees, adapted themselves remarkably well to the new conditions. The opening match against Leigh, away, showed conclusively that our lads had practically mastered the intricacies by giving a very creditable display which was satisfactory under the trying condi- tions—the afternoon being the hottest known for some years and in many instances causing the kick-off to be dslaied until 3.30. This confounded the opinion advanced by many that the game would be too fast and players could not go through 80 minutes play, as ours were not unduly fatigued at the finish of a hard and punishing match. Des- cribing some of the matches Mr. Ashton says: Our 1" A "team turned out to oppose Halifax on Good IFrictay and gave them a fine game, only losing by 5 to 3. The reason for taking such action as to reserve all the , first team players for the day following to oppose Huddersfield away in the 3rd round of the Northern Union Cup, and the satisfactory result justified such policy. Easter Monday saw Leeds giving us a good show and a pleasant game though they were defeated by a large score. Our mach at Huddersfield reversed the result of the previous meeting. In the semi-final for the Northern Union Cup we had to encounter Swinton at Wigan, and, though easily defeating them, it was not a meritorious display, possibly accounted for by the wet and dirty state of the ground, a heavy shower falling just before the start. Having adminis- tered a beating to Rochdale we came to the last match of a very busy season. A fitting termination was our experience as contestants with Oldham in the final for the honour of holding of the Northern Union Cup. This was our fourth meeting during the season, losing the two League games and singular to relate winning both Cup-ties. A keen and particularly exciting contest showed showed our players to be in the very pink of condition.

The" A "team have performed fairly well generally, although they failed to again win the Lancashire Com- bination championship. They experienced some cruel ill-luck on several occasions. Wigan away was a case in point. The Warrington men were leading practically up to the call of time, when a serious mistake committed by one of our team through foolishness, allowed Wigan to score and convert, virtnally pulling the match out of the fine. Salford beat us but the loss of one of our most promising players, D. Lambert, who met with a nasty injury, accounted greatly for our defeat. Altogether 22 matches were played, 17 won, 4 lost and 1 drawn.

The works medal competition proved a most striking success—absolutely the most successful in the history of the Competition—and although fortune has not hestowed upon us many promising juniors, the Competition has been the means of affording would-Se aspirants the opportunity to display their ability. Besides a record in point of number of entries (31), a record was broken for the final, there being a remarkably fine attendance of 6,000 and gate money reaching £36. This amount was very pleasing, seeing that only 2d. and 4d. were the charges of admission. The class of football was also good, many of the teams showing some really fine play. Several of the games were of a very interesting character' this being due in some degree to the reforms In the rules of the game. Lease of Ground.—Your Committee with a view of obtaining a renewal of the lease of the ground approached Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company,and it is gratifying to be able to state that a satisfactory understanding has been arrived at. 1 Changes in the Game.—The reduction in the number of players has been tbe means -Of curtailing expenses somewhat, but apart froni'that it has afforded oppor- tunities of much brighter football, less observation of the ball, besides preventing many of the abuses exist- ing under the old order. Play the ball rule was a very Idebateable question in the early part of the season, lowing to no uniformity on the part of referees, and the pla)ers themselves suffered, there being no general system for the proper administration of the rule. However, a sub-committee drafted a series of instruc- tions to referees and to Club Committees by which means a more satisfactory state of things was gradually effected. Penalties for touch kicking brought about much more open play, stopping that detestable feature so common last season of constantly finding touch, and affording frequent opportunities of having the ball to play with, while the forwards had ample chances of handling to show their skill.

Candidly I feel such reforms have tended to generally improve our game, making it faster, with possibilities of more attractive play. League Reforms.—A further reconstruction of the League in certain to be accomplished, and next season will see a Lancashire and Yorkshire County League, on the principle of 2 points for a win and one for a draw, with a Northern Union League on the percentage system, _ _

The Treasurer (Mr. T. PEMBUITON) presents the fol- lowing statement :—I have the pleasure to submit to you the accounts for the past season, showing a great improvement in the financial stinding of the club. The membership has :main increaseJ, the number being 920, against 852 at the end of season 1905-6.

div.head: WONDERFUL ANNUAL.
div.p: A WONDERFUL ANNUAL.
" Printer's Ple-1907."

"Printers' Pie" has now become a hardy annual. Founded four years ago by Mr. W. Hugh Spottiswoode, with the assistance of Mr. Arthur Croxton, the editor of" The Tatler," " Printers' Pie" is issued to benefit the funds of the Printers' Pension. Almshouse and Orphan Asylum Corporation. The first issue of "Printers' Pie" was published at 2s. 6d., and 10,000 copies were sold. In 1904 the annual was published at is., when 25,000 copies were disposed of. In 1905 the entire edition of 40,000 copies at is. was sold out within a fortnight of publication' whilst in 1906 50,000 copies were sold out in two days. This year Mr. Spottiswoode is printing 100,000 copies. The present issue is particularly attractive and con- tains contributions from Kaharine Tynan, G. R. Sims, Adrian Ross, W. Pett Ridge, Frank Richardson, William Le Queux,T. Mostyn Pigott, Barry Pain, Lord Montagu, H. W. Lucy, E. V. Lucas, Cosmo Hamilton, C. L. Graves' Tom Gallon, Athol Forbes, H. Hamilton Fyfe, Austin Dobson, Lieut.-Colonel Newnham-Davis, Gerald Campbell, D. C. Calthrop, G. B. Burgin J. M. Bulloch, the Duke of Argyll, K.T., F. Anstey, and W. L. Alden. A great feature this year is that all the illustrations are printed in colours. They include drawings by—John Hassall, Lawson Wood, Charles Folkard, F. H. Townsend, Starr Wood, Tom Browne' Savile Lumley, H. M. Bateman, Charles Crombie, Dudley Buxton, Charles Pear; G. D. Armour, Cecil Aldin, H. M. Brock, Will Owen, David Wilson, Lewis Baumer, George Belcher, E. T. Reed, Gunning King, and Fred Pegram. In recognition of the efforts of the booksellers and net/magenta of the country, a qontribution will be again made, from the procaeds of the forthcoming issue, to the Funds of he Booksellers' Provident Institution and the Newsvendors' Benevolent and Provident Institution. Another great feature of this issue is that it carries with it a Free 1,000 Insurance, for three months, against accidents to passengers in motor 'buses, electric trams, &c._

div.head: Old Man's Sad Fate.
div.p: Old Man's Sad Fate.

At the Warrington Police Conrt on Tuesday, an old man Sergeant Richards, 9, Pinners-brow, was charged with having attempted to commit suicide.—Superin- tendent Monaghan stated that prisoner was .74 years of age, and was formerly an ironworker, but for the last two years had not followed any employment. He had an income sufficient to keep him, and this was paid to him onoe a week by a gentleman in town. A week before prisoner attempted to commit suicide the gentleman in question told him the money was getting exhausted, and there was nothing for him but the workhouse when the money was done. This seemed to upset prisoner very much and on April 25th his landlady found him lying on the bed with his throat cut' Prisoner was very sorry for what he had done. He promised to do nothing of the kind again, and as he was willing to go into the Workhouse, he (the Superintendent) wished to withdraw the charge against him. -Mr. W. Hickman said Richards was an epileptit and if the Bench could see their way to make a permanent order for prisoner to be kept in the Work- house, in the epileptic department, it would be the best thing that could be done for him.—The Beilch then committed prisoner to the workhouse.

THE MAGPIE'S LESSON TO THE BIRDS.

Once there was a great stir among the birds. Word went round that the Magpie had found a new way of making a nest, with a cover over the top to keep off the rain. Some other birds were anxious to learn how to do this; so tire), asked the Magpie to give them a lesson. "I cannot spare much time," she replied. "You see, I have my little ones to teed; but if you come all at one time, I will show you. So all the birds came to one end of the wood. Some perched on branches; others sat on the ground, and, after much flapping of wings, they were ready. "Now," began the Magpie, "you first choose a forked branch in a tree-"
"We all know that," chirped the Robins and Finches.
"Oh, no," said the Lark; "the ground is the better place. Then your nest does not get blown down by the wind." "No, but it may be trodden on by some animal, and-"
"Oh, please let me go on," said the Magpie. "Next, you lay two- sticks across, like this." • "Yes, yes," said the Jackdaw. "Common- sense would teach me that I must begin like that."

"Will you kindly allow me to proceed? I shall never finish if you interrupt me go." "O-r-d-er ! 04)-o-r-der! r cawed the rooks, who had been making more noise than anyone. "Our youngest bird knows this." "Now," went on the Magpie.; "straw next, and weave round this way."
"Don't stop; we all know that," raid the Crow.
"Now," went on the 'Magpie an,:e more, "you take hay and moss, and begin to line the nest."
"Anyone could guess that, without being taught," chirped the Sparrow. "More moss, then feathers, or anything soft-"
"I prefer thistledown," murmured the Finch. "Place them inside, so."
"Who would be silly enough to put them outsider said the Swallow.

By this time the Magpie was disgusted. "If you know 'so much, why did you ask me to teach you?" she said; and flew away, leaving the nest only half finished. Moral: Those who are too wise to be taught never learn anything worth knowing.
ANNIE ST-lIETTON.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sending you a story (written by myself) for your "Children's Corner." I hope it will be successful in gain- ing a prise. Please would you send me a bottle of Mason's Extract of Herbs? I will say no more now. HARGREAVES PARKINSON. WHAT MOTHER BROUGHT.

Kitty Johnstone was at the window, looking expectantly out into the street. The rain was falling, and the streets were very muddy. But Kitty was looking for her mother, who had gone out shopping, and had promised to bring something nice fOr Kitty. Kitty, being the only one in the house, was a bit frightened, but the feeling passed away as she thought of mother's present. "It might be a doll, or a doll's house," mused Kitty. "If it is a doll, I will call it 'Miss Anne Jones'; if it is a doll's house, I will call the house 'Rose Villa."

• Kitty's reflections were cut short by someone opening the door, and then mother ent2red. Kitty gave a cry of joy, and wa.s soon untying a hamper, when out came a little kitten—such a nice one, too; and Kitty was delighted. The kitten is quite a big one now, and Kitty loves it very much. H. P.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l write these few lines, hoping you are well. You will think I am a long time in writing. Will you please smd me a bottle of Meson's Extract of Herbs? I am also sending you a short story, entitled:

div.head: MY DEAR NIECES AND NEPHEWS,
div.p: MY DEAR NIECES AND NEPHEWS,

Last week I think I was in a very grumbling mood, wasn't I? As I told you, the rain was raining every day, and now, to day—what a change—bright, beautiful summer-time, and how radiant everybody looks! surprising what influence nice weather has over us. In an instant, it turns tears to smiles, grave to gay, and mud to dust. BUT, let us not be too joy- ful; we must remember that we a.ro in England —where the climates come from—and to-morrow it may SNOW! Let us hope not! Well, my dears, I have received a good pile of letters this week; but I am afraid I cannot publish as many as I should like. I am now putting more into the "Corner" than I should do, and then only by clipping down some of the letters. I was quite surprised to get so many applications for Mason's delicious Extract of Herbs; this in itself is the sign of approach- ing summer. Well, it's a very healthy, pure drink, and I only wish that more of it was drunk in the place of its evil-dealing alcoholic rival. I don't mind the tiniest bit how many bottles I give away of Mason's—cartloads, if it's asked for—because I know that it's a splendid strengthening beverage for all you growing girls and boys. The prize for the first opened solu- tion of "Hidden Foods" goes to Bertha Lister-- to whom it has been despatched. Good-bye for smother seven days. 'UNCLE NED.

A Cambridge Professor once asked one of his friends to lend him a book, which he wished to consult. The messenger returned with the following answer: "I never allow my books to be taken out of my study; but if you like to come there, you are welcome to read as long as you please." Some days after this, the friend applied to the Professor for the loan of his bellows. Remembering the refusal he had lately met with, he replied: "I never allow my bellows to be taken out of my room; but if you choose to come there, you are welcome to blow with them as long as you like!"
TOM EDMUND JESSOP

A hungry fox, returning homeward one winter afternoon from a fruitless visit to the rabbit-warren, spied two fine hares, lying in the shelter of a broken fence. "What good luck 1" said he, joyfully, to himself. "Now I shall not go without supper to bed." Peering through a gap in the fence, he looked thought- fully from one to the other. "Which shall I take?" mused he "Jack is the larger, but Puss is the plumpepr. Jack would be the more full-flavoured; Puss might be the easier to catch. But then, if I let Jack go now, I may Dever find him again, whereas if Puss is left without her mate, she will be easily deceived. I think it shall be Jack." He was about to spring through the gap, when his eye fell once more upon Puss. He paused. "How fat she is!" thought he; "and how tender she would be! After all, I will choose Puss." Just then, Jack looked round. "A fox! a fox!!" squeaked he. In a moment the hares were half-way across the next field. "I wish I had taken Jack!" panted the fox, as he followed far behind. ANNIE BATEMAN.

"Please give me a penny, sir; My mother dear is dead. And, oh, I am so hungry, sir— A penny, please, for bread. "All day I have been asking, But no one hears my cry; Will you not give me something? Or, surely, I must die. "Please give me a penny, sir; You won't say 'No' to me, -3ecause I'm poor and ragged, sir, And, oh, so cold, you see I "We were not always begging— We once were rich, like you; But father died a drunkard, And mother—she died, too."

div.head: EAGLE AND THE CROW.
div.p: THE EAGLE AND THE CROW.

An eagle flew down from the top of a high rock and settled on the back of a lamb, 6.nd then, instantly flying into the air again, bore the prize heavenwards. A crow, sitting on an elm, beheld this exploit, and resolved to imitate the eagle, anol, flying down on the back of a ram, entangled its claws in the wool, and attempted to fly. The shepherd saw this, and caught the crow and gave it to his boys for- their sport and diversion.
J. RICHARDSON.
- TWO LITTLE KITTENS.
Two little kittens, One stormy night, Began to quarrel, And then to fight.
One had a mouse, And the other had none; And that was the way The quarrel begun.
"I'll have that mbuse," Said the bigger cat. "You'll have that mouse? We'll see about that."

"I will have that mouse," Said the tortoise-shell; And, spitting and scratching, On her sister she fell. The old woman took The sweeping broom, And swept them both Right out ol the room. The ground was covered With frost and snow; They had lost the mouse, And had nowhere to go.
