div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.

Walker—Dodds. The Wesleyan Church at Penketh was the scene of • a very pretty wedding on Thursday afternoon, the contracting parties being Miss Annie Dodds, eldest daughter of Mr. James Dodds, Penketh House, Penketh, and Mr. Edward Valentine Walker, editor of the " Examiner "and only son of the late Mr. John Walker, Latchford. Great interest was taken in the event and a very large congregatioa assemb'ed, the church being filled to its utmost capacity. Fortunately the weather was beautifully fine and the arrival of the guests and the bridal paety was watched with interest by crowds of well-wishers who lined the approaches to the church. The interior of the building looked very beautiful, being decorated most artistically with lilies, narcissi and other choice flowers. Mr. George Weaver presided at the organ and while the „guests were assembling played appropriate selec- tions. Promptly at two o'clock the bride entered the church leaning on the arm of her father by whom she was given away. She was charmingly .attired in a white satin dress, the bodice being trimmed with chiffon and real lace, and the skirt with .chiffon and white heather. She wore a veil of rich net surmounted with a pretty wreath of myrtle and orange blossoms, and carried a lovely bouquet of white roses, lilies of the valley, lilium candichim, gardenias and stephanotis. Her ornaments were a pair of gold bracelets, the gift of the bridegroom. 'There were three bridesmaids :—Miss Adelaide Mary Dodds and Miss Marjorie Dodds (sisters of the bride) and Miss Clarice Walker (sister of the bridegroom). Their dresses were of Paris lace over chiffon and chiffon taffeta, trimmed with net. They wore cream coloured areophane and crinoline hats, trimmed with large pink and damask roses, Nvith ends of velvet and areophane, and, carried bouquets of dark red roses and lilies of the valley. Their gold brooches were the gifts of the bridegroom. Dr. W. Briggs, Black- burn, acted as best man. The service was conducted by the Rev. John Gunnell, who has long been associated with Wesleyan Methodist work in Penketh. The ch@ir was in attendance, and the hymns "The voice that breathed o'er Eden" and "0 Perfect Love " were sung. At the close of the ceremony the organist played the " Bridal Chorus" from " Lohengrin ' and as the bridal party left the church the joyous strains of Mendelssohn's " Wedding March" pealed forth. The reception was held at Penketh House, and a large number of guests attended. Refreshments were served in a marquee in the grounds. The newly-married couple, who were the recipients of hearty congratulations and good wishes, departed later in the day for the East Coast of Ireland, where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress was a blue cloth toilette, with light and dark green satin straw hat trimmed with shaded flowers.
During the afternoon a number of congratulatory telegrams were received,includinq one from Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., and one from Mr. C. E. Parker.

On Tuesday evening -a deputition from the Warring- ton Municipal Association visited Penk-eth House to make a presentation to Miss Dodds, as some recognition of her father's work for that Association and for the town of Warrington. The present took the form of a unique and handsome chiming clock, afhxed to the base of which was a silver plate bearing the following inscrip- tion :—" Presented to Miss Dodds on the occasion of her marriage, May 16th, 1907, by a few friends as a token of their esteem and as an acknowledgment of her father's public work for the 'welfare of Warrington." Messrs. Kenyon and Horrocks made the presentation, which was acknowledged-by both Miss Dodds and her father. Mr. Dodds has since forwarded the following letter to the Secretary of the Warrington Municpal Association :

Penketh House, near Warrington. May 14th, 19.07. Dear Mr. Kenyon,—l cannot refrain from writing to thank my " Non-Trading" colleagues for the most handsome present they have sent to my daughter on the occasion of her marriage and especially for their kind and generous reference in the inscription to my humble share in the work theyand I have together accomplished for Warrington. If there is anything of which I am proud, or in respect of which I should prefer to be remembered, it is my association over the past six or seven years with the few men who so disinterestedly and so effectually stood for, and secured purity and probity in the municipal life of our town. I am, dear Mr. Kenyon, yours sincerely, JAM ES DODDS,

div.head: S. KENYON, ESQ. PRESENTATION FROM " EXAMINER " EMPLOYEES.
div.p: S. KENYON, ESQ. PRESENTATION FROM " EXAMINER " EMPLOYEES.

There was a pleasing little ceremony at the " Examiner " Office, when Mr. E. V. Walker was the ree'pient of a wedding present from the employees. The presentation was made in the works by Mr. Henry Bond (manager) in the presence of a full gathering. Mr. BOND said that as the senior member of the " Examiner " staff it fell to his lot to voice the senti- ments of the office in regard to Mr. Walker's approach- ing marriage—an event in which they all took a deep interest. It had been felt that they could not allow so happy and auspicious an event to pass without some suitable recognition, and to him therefore had been deputed the pleasant duty of presentinc, to Mr. Walker a little wedding gift, towards which each and every one of the employees had quite enthusiastically contributed. He thought he would be expressing the minds of all present when he said that they wished Mr, Walker to regard the present as a slight token of the high esteem in which he was held by all his workpeople, and as a testimonial also of the good feeling which existed, and had always existed between them as employer and employed. (Applause). Some of them whose memory went back, as his (Mr. Bond's) did, to the time when the late Mr. John Walker directed the affairs of the "Examiner "recalled with both pleasure and pride the many admirable qualities which he had undoubtedly handed on to his son and heir. He alluded not only to Mr. E. V. Walker's proved abilities as a literary man, but more especially to that sympathetic and kindly interest in the welfare of his workpeople which characterised his disposition and which was always so warmly appreciated by servants in regard to employers. (Applause). He (Mr. Bond) was sure all present joined with him in wishing that Mr. Walker might long be spared to conduct and control the newspaper with which his father's name was so brilliantly associated. Mr. Bond concluded by asking Mr. Walker to accept a case of solid silver salt cellars with the united best wishes of the staff for the happi- ness and prosperity of his married life, and with the expression of the hope that the future might have in store many blessings for him and for the future Mrs. E. V. Walker. (Applause). Mr. E. IDDON (chief reporter) cordially endorsed the sentiments expressed by Mr. Bond and also testified to the pleasant relations which existed between Mr. Walker and his staff. Their sincere good wishes went forth to Mr. Walker and the bride elect that they might enjoy good health, long life and the fullest measure of happiness. (Applause.) . .

div.head: DEATH OF MR. E. W. CLARKE.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. E. W. CLARKE.

A painful sensation was created locally on Monday by the sudden death of Mr. Edwin Wright Clarke, which occurred at his residence,Oakleigh,Great Sankey,shortly before noon. The deceased gentleman who was 45 years of age, had been in declining health for some time though his death was altogether unexpected. On Friday he was at business, and not feeling very well consulted Dr. Joseph, who advised complete rest. On Monday morning Mr. Clarke rallied somewhat,and was preparing to leave his bedroom when he collapsed and died in about an hour from hmmorrhage of the brain. A native of Lostock Gralam, Mr. Clarke came to Penketh about 19 years ago, to take charge of the Post °Moe. He subsequently occupied high positions at Horwich, near Bolton, St. Helens and Widnes, and in the year 1900, through the influence of Mr. James Dodds, he became the manager of the colliery department of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Ltd., in Tanners-lane, Warrington. His excellent business capacity soon earned for him the respect of the firm and the customers generally. He was a Liberal in politics, and a Church- man. He was a member of the " Equity " Lodge of , Freemasons (1384), Widnes, and of the " Gilbert 1 Greenall "Lodge (1250), Warrington. He also took a ' great interest in cricket, and was hon. treasurer of the Penketh Cricket Club. In Warrington he was wldely known and was extremely popular. He seemed always Lto look on the bright side of things and his unvarying 'cheerfulness won for him a host of friends by whom his untimely end will be sincerely regretted. Much sympathy has been extended to the widow and family in their, bereavement.

The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Wednes- day amid many manifestations of respect. In addition to the relatives there were also present: Mr. James Dodd g (representing Messrs. Pearson, Knowles and Co.), Messrs. T. Gerrard and T. Wright (Wigan), R. Ridpath, R. Barlow, T. Hankey, J. Leigh, W. Heesom and A. Balmer. Lodge Equity 1334 (Widnes) of Freemasons was represented by Bros. F. Sherratt, W.M., W. Lowe, T.P.M., J. S. Potter, P.n., P.Z., P.P.G.5.8., T. Showan, P.M., P.Z., J. Sadler, S.D., R. Strickland, g., F'. Taylor, T. Cooper, J. H. Daintith, W. H. Ireland, P. Lawton, T. Sadler, R. Taylor, J. Ambrose, C. Evans, W. McCurie W. R. Laws, T. Fox, R. G. Gow, J. Williams, and S. Welding, whilst the Gilbert Greenall Lodge was repre- sented by Bros. W. Whittaker, P.M., M.E.Z., R. Lunt, P.M., W. Hodgkiilson, P.M., S.N., J. R. Griffiths, P.M., P.Z., J. Clay, P.M., P.Z., J. Waldron, S.E., T. Healing S.W., A.S., C. B. Aylward and F.J. Dell. The ceremony was conducted by the Revs. J. Gunnell and J. R. Jones. Amongst the many beautiful flOral tributes which were placed on the grave were wreaths from Mr. Ridpath and the employees at the Tanners-lane yard, the dealers, and from Messrs. Pearson and Knowles and Co..

div.head: EMPIRE DAY.
div.p: EMPIRE DAY.
Local Celebrations.

Yesterday wag Empire Day and its advent was signalized locally by a generous display of flags and bunting, patriotic emblems being prominent at all the public and semi-public buildings. The day had a greater significance than ever for the children of the town and at all the senior elementary schools the occasion was made one for special rejoicing. Recently the. Mayor offered to present a number of medals and brooches for the most popular boys and girls in the various schools the recipients being selected by the children themselves. The distribution was made personally by his Worshsp who drove to the different institutions in a motor car placed at his disposal by Dr. Markel. He was accompanied by the Mayoress, Alderman Bennett, Mr. G. H. Kingdon, Mr. J. Moore Murray and the Rev.. W. Bracecamp Most of the schools had been specially decorated for the visit and in some instances the display of bunting was most elaborate. At each school the Mayor briefly addressed the children impressing upon them the duty 'of true patriotism. At the secondary school appor- tunity was taken of placing before the children a special lesson in regard to their duty to their town and with this object a number of photographs of local gentlemen, including those of the Borough Member, Mr. A. H. Crosfleld, and the Mayor were on view, the services rendered by each to tho town being explained. The children at the different centres sang a number of patriotic songs whilst at the Secondary School a special programme of songs, recitations &c., was submitted. During the day the Mayoress was presented with a number of beautiful bouquets whilst the boys I from St. Mary's School handed a ham:some silver I matchbox to Alderman Smethurst. ' The recipients of the various medals were:— PEOPLE'S COLLEGE.—Susie Fish and John Milburn. SACRED HEART.—Albert Houghton and Lily Riley. ST. BARNADAS'.—Thomas Forster and Mary Grounds. WYCLIFFE.—CharIes Bennett and Clara Holland. HEATHSIDE.—Frank Fern, and Maggie Woodward. ST. ALBA.N'S.—John Coleman and Margaret Stump. ST. MARY'S.—John Hill and Kate Murphy. LADIES' SCHOOL OF INDUSTRY.—AIice Clough. 1 ST. JAMES'.—Harold Greenhalgh and Marion Dawes. LATCHFORD R.C.—Peter Burke and Dora Carter. CHRIST CHURCH.—GeraId Doncaster and Minnie Wells.
ST. ANN'S (Senior).—Fiank Bonnel and Minnie Bonnel.
S. A's (Junior).--Charles Glover and Beatrice Bonnel.
SILVER-STREET.—Frank Kent and John Leigh. HAMILTON-STREET.— Fred Pilling and Dorothy Plins- ton.

ST7gEDEDICT'S.—rhomas Mannion and Ada Archer. BEAMONT SCHOOL.—George Weaver and Ivy Wilkinson FAIRFIELD HIGHER GRADE.—Hettie Shaw. FAIRFIELD.—Dorothy Wainwright. PAROCHIAL.—John Metcalf. TRINITY.—Wm. Saunders and Hilda Gleave. PULPIT REFERENCES.

Empire Day was the subject of several references ' from Warrington pulpits on Sunday, from which we give brief extracts. At St. Peter's Church the Rev. H. A. Lester said true Imperialism was not a desire to be acquiring mere material profit, gain of gold, increase of territory; it was rather the impulse to be giving, com- ' municating and bestowing on the less-favoured races , the gifts which they had so bountifully received. At Latchford Baptist Church the Rev. J. F. MATTHEWS said he hoped that parents would never consent to that piece of flunkeyism known as saluting the flag when practised, nor would they ever consent to the creation of rifle corps in secondary schools, a sug- gestion, he believed, that had emanated .from Lord Meath's Committee. Ours was not a military Empire. Supreme justice should be ideal in our administra- tive life and it must mark our attitude and conduct to the smaller coloured non-English speaking races within our domain.

The Rev. C. L: STOWE at Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church urged his hearers to look beyond the bounds of Empire and do something for the relief of less-fortunate people, such as the inhabitants of the Congo. 0

AC Bold-street Wesleyan Church, the Rev. J. Manning said they shared the glories and privileges of the Empire and ought to be equally anxious to discharge it duties, to bear its responsibilities. Loyalty meant facing the problems of this Empire, and doing one's share in making the nationallife sweet and strong.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH. _ Newcastle-on-Tyne Doctor Appointed.
div.p: THE MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH. _ Newcastle-on-Tyne Doctor Appointed.

The Health Committee of the Warrington Corpora- tion met on Wednesday to appoint a medical officer of health for the borough in succession to the late Dr. J. Guest Go'rnall. 'Originally there were 26 applicants and tho following were selected to appear before the committee :—Dr. James Bennett, Padgate, Dr. Daley, Bootle: Dr. Goldsmith, Manchester; Dr. Hodgson, Halifax ; Dr. J. Coote Hibbert, Newcastle-on-Tyne ; Dr. Laird, Crewe; Dr. Rock, Huddersfield. Dr. Bennett, we are informed, made his application with a certain reservation, intimating that if the condition could not be acceded to his application must be con- sidered withdrawn.

1- The choice of the committee fell upon Mr. J. Coote Hibbert, M.D. (Load.), L.R.C.P. (Loud.), M.R.C.S. (Eng,), 'D.Ph. (Load.), of Newcastle-on-Tyne. He is thirty-five years of age and studied medicine at the ' University College Hospital, London, where after obtaining his degree he continued to work for several i years and held most of the resident appointments. ; On leaving University College, he acted for several months as resident medical officer of the North- Western Fever Hospital under the Metropolitan d For the last five years he has Ad‘e7ohmtleds Board entirely to public health work and ! has studied under the medical officers of health Ifor the County of Glamorgan and the County IBorough and Port of Cardiff. Having obtained the diploma in Public Health be acted for a year as assistant and deputy to the medical officer for Cardiff, During that time he was also assistant bacteriologist at Cardiff and was connected with the public health labortmy where he assisted in carrying out for Glamorgan and Cardiff bacteriological investigations for the diagnosis of infectious disease and bacterio- logical examinations of water supplies, food, &c. He • subsequently held the appointment of temporary medical officer to the Rhondda Urban District Council and a similar office at Southampton. At the presentl time he is assistant and deputy medical officer to the City of Newcastle-on-Tyne and resident medical officer at the city hospital for infectious diseases, which post he has held for two and a half years. He is also in charge under the medici l! officer of health of the city small-pox hospital and isolation hospital for " contacts' where over 200 cases of small-pox have been under his care. He is thoroughly familiar with all the departments of health and sanitary administration.

div.head: CUP VICTORY.
div.p: THE CUP VICTORY.
Players Entertained at Walton Hall.

The celebrations of the success of Warrington in the Northern Union Cup final were continued last evening when the players were the guests of Sir Gilbert Greenall who entertained them to dinner at Walton Hall. The repast was served in the riding school which had been specially decorated for the occasion by Mr. Ralph Johnson. Alternately the windows were hung with primrose and blue curtains, whilst a platform at one end had been artistically draped with the Warring- ton Club colours surmounted by the Royal Arms national emblems and flags. In the centre the Cup was prominently displayed on a pedestal and surrounded by a beautiful bank of flowers, the tables being arranged either side in the shape of a huge horseshoe. Sir Gilbert Greenall presided, and amongst those present were :—The Mayor, Messrs. %Vnitley, W. Bain- bridge, J. H. Clarke. R. J. Wynne-Jones, E. Draper, J E. Seeker. Henry Greenall, John White, Councillor Fulton Smith, E. J. Hall, C. %V. Wilson, J. E. Warren (president of the club), El. Ashton (hon. secretary), and members of the flub Committee.
The catering was in the hands of Mr. Powis, who did justice to an excellent menu. . .. _
- After dinner the evening was enjoyably spent in speech-making, pleasant I y interspered with song. To-day (Saturday), Mr. A. H. Crosfleld, 51.. P, enter- tains the team at Chester.

div.head: Fatal Fall.
div.p: Fatal Fall.

Mr. S. Brighouse conducted an inquest on Wednes- day at the Warrington Police Station on the body of Sarah Beatrice Warburton Plumpton, aged 30, 1, FairClough's-yard, Bridge Foot, who died on Monday from injuries received on the previous night through falling from the bedroom window. The husband of the deceased stated that for some time past his wife had been in very delicate health, and last week suffered from a severe attack of influenza. On Sunday he remained with her all day, but left her for a few minutes to go downstairs. On his return he missed her, sod looking through the window he saw her lying on the flags in the yard below. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

div.head: COLONIAL PREFERENCE.
div.p: COLONIAL PREFERENCE.
[BY MR. C. E. PARKER].

I have no desire- to impute to that, section of our Colonists who are asking the Mother onntry. to alter her fiscal policy, motives other than patriotic and imperial. But while they may honestly believe that their proposals if carried out would be for the benefit of the whole Empire I venture to submit that they are unfair and specially unjust to the Mother Country. In the first place, they claim the right to maintain a tariff high enough to protect their own manufactures which have been developed under and depend upon a protective system, against effective competition with British manufacturers; and second while they already have an absolutely free market in the United Kingdom even where they compete with our own products they claim that we should further give them preferential treatment in our market by erecting a tariff that will exclude a considerable quantity of foreign products, food and raw material, so that more room may bs made for Colonial products. Mr. Deakin tells us that Great Britain uses articles which Australia can supply amounting to £213,000,000. Of these Australia at present supplies £10,000,000, other British possessions including India £40;000,000, and foreign countries £160,000,000. We are to put impediments in the way of a trade represented by £160,000 for the sake of increasing the £50,000,000. Can Australia and other self-governing bodies supply any large proportion of this £160,000,000, and would they supply them at the old price in the absence of competition on equal terms? Again what have the Colonies to offer us that will make a sacrifice on our part worth while? The possibil- ity of developing a largely increased trade with the colonies in manufactures is comparatively small. The ' tariff barriers are left high enough to protect and develop their own manufactures. Apart from this their 'population is comparatively small, the world's market is far larger,and therefore of greater importance to usit is a question of eleven million customers against several hundred millions. This question is in the main a quanti- tative one, and it is folly to allow the sentiment of the question to blur and distort our sense of proportion. The colonies ask of us infinitely more than they are prepared to grant to us. What they grant will benefit a few special trades, and what we are asked to grant would be a burden on the whole population. The British Empire is not in any sense an Empire in the way in which the world has hitherto used the word. It is a union of republics possessing practical indepen- idence under one crown, each unit of which has followed its own line of development. To unite these into fiscal unity' based on Free Trade within the Empire would be a laudable object, but the Protectionist system which the colonies have adopted (and which the mother country has left thorn free to adopt) has made it impos- sible to consolidate the Empire by any equitable system of fiscal unity. To attempt it on an unequal footing, that is, for the mother country to allow colonial goods in free, and to be obliged to tax our other purchases of food and raw material, while our manufactures have no free entrance into the Colonies would be altogether one- sided, and specially unfair to the mother country. Further in the event of Colonial Preference being adopted, and foreign nations offering us con- cessions to induce us to abstain from raising taxes upon their trade what is to become of the retaliation principle so dear to tariff reformers? Would we have to "slam the door in the face "of any country desiring to negotiate? We will have tied our hands, because if we arrange separate tariffs with any foreign country the value of the preference of the Colonies becomes of less value to them, who presumably have an arrange- ment with us to give them an advantage by taxing imports of foreign origin for a definite preference in the Colonial markets. In this way the two branches of fiscal reform come into collision. Freedom to negotiate and permanent preference cannot work in unison. It would be like a man whose legs want to go opposite ways. • It is one of the principles of protection legislation that food and raw materials should be admitted free and that no tax should be put on materials manu- factured or otherwise, which are not produced, or pro- duced in limited quantities in the country adopting the protective system. Apart from the Colonial questlon Tariff Reformers would start at the manufac- turing end,and only a few extremists would tax food andl raw material. The goods which the Colonists send us are mainly of this character, and we are asked to apply the system in a way which on the admission of most Protectionists is injurious, or at any rate a beginning, at the wrong end. The only Preference which would be of any use to the Colonies would be duties on raw materials and food stuffs. This would imperil the advantage which our Free Trade system gives us, for by it we garner the bargains of the world, by it we feed our people, and feed them well and at a low cost, by it we run the blockades ot tariff barriers by cheap , production, and by ships built and equipped at rates which no protectionist country can approach. To tax the necessaries of life or livelihood which we cannot produce, and which the Colonies cannot produce in sufficient quantities for many years (even if stimulated by higher prices due to Preference in the homeldnd) would be an act of injustice to our people, and a serious handicap to those trades which depend for their con- tinued prosperity upon a world-wide free market for their materials for production. CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketb. 14th May, 1907.

div.head: NEXT OPERA. '
div.p: THE NEXT OPERA. '
"The Yeomen of the Guard."

I The decision of the Opera Committee of the War- ! riagton Musical Society to repeat in October next the opera in which, fout years ago, they scored such a signal initial success, will doubtless be hailed with pleasurable satisfaction by the groat bulk of that numerous public which has enjoyed each and all of the good things that enterprising body has laid before them. Popular vote leaves little doubt that of the bunch of the Gilbert and Sullivan collaborations this is indeed "the pick." Nor is there much doubt that, splendidly as" The Yeomen of the Guard "was presented on the first occasion, the forthcoming six nights' run will indicate an advance in the ability of all concerned to pourtray these inimitable specimens of" light," or, as it is more popularly known, "comic" opera. With two exceptions the whole of the "principals" will again appear in their respective roles, the changes involved being, as will be seen from list of dramatis personae given below, the replacing of Miss Emily D.Jeans (who is not now a member of the society) as "Dame Carruthers," by Miss Garnett Ball who so ably portrayed the part of the" Fairy Queen" in "lolanthe" last year, and the assumption of the part of "Leonard Meryll " by Mr. J. E.Hannan who it will be remembered greatly distinguished himself three years ago as " Luiz " in "The Gondoliers." Rehearsals of the chorus are now in full swing under the able direction of Mr. F. H. Crossley, and we understand that great enthusiasm is being shown in the study of the Yeomen choruses of which many pleasant memories doubtless survive amongst those members who took part in the first performances. Appended to the list of principal personages are the names of the members of the chorus.

div.head: BREAD WITII CURRANTS IN.
div.p: BREAD WITII CURRANTS IN.

This according to the King's Physician, is a most nutritious, easily digestible, and altogether healthful food. The currant loaf that is twenty-four hours old is the best for cutting, and children as well as adults should be allowed the luxury of very thin slices. The main object of this thin slicing is to cut through the currants so that the full benefit of their flavour is given to the bread.
LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES.

The daily sailings to North Wales will be consider- ably augmented for the Whitsuntide holidays. Yester- day (Friday), the St. Elvies made her first trip of the season, and opened up the regular daily service to and from Menai Bridge; whilst commencing to-day (Satur- day), the well-known and popular steamer La Marguerite will take her place for Whit-week, running daily until the 27th May. Anglesey excursions are also announced by the St. Tudno on Whit Sunday, Whit Monday, and NVhit Tuesday. Given fine weather, there is no more popular excursion on the coast than this health-giving and pleasurable sea excursion of 180 miles of coast scenery, combined with the excellent catering,which go a long way to make a sea trip enjoyable. On Whit Monday three sailings are advertised,viz.. by St. Elvies, for Llandudno (6 hours ashore), Beaumaris, Bangor. and Menai Bridge, with Carnarvon connection by Snowdon; also the Anglesey trip, as mentioned, by St. Tvdno, and La 'Marguerite for Llandudno, Beaumaris, Bangor, and Menai Bridge, due back at 7.30 p.m.

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CENTENARY.
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CENTENARY.
A BRIEF HISTORY.
[Continued front last week.]

Before his visit to Mow Cop in 1800, however, Hugh Bourne had joined the Methodist Church, for that he should join some Church was a settled conviction with him. His first feeling as he looked around the degraded neighbourhood was not, "What a fine field of usefulness is here," but rather a fear lest he himself should succumb to the evils of the place. There was only the one little chapel already mentioned anywhere near, and there seemed absolute famine of the Word of Life. Bourne longed for more congenial surround- ings and wished that his business could have been concluded at once. But instead of loosing him Providence chaine .1 him to the spot. First he was asked to undertake the woodwork of a mountain farm, and secondly to do the same for Stonetrough Colliery, nor did he see how he could refuse either contract. It was a good thing for Hugh Bourne that his longings for his native means of grace were unrealised, for his own new religious life became a robaster thing by his ministry to others, and by his ministry again he was made to overcome some of the timidity and reserve of his shy and serious nature. His first venture was to broach the subject of experimental religion to the zillage smith, and to finish his daring visit by putting 3 written account of his own conversion into the smith's bands. Then on Christmas Day 1800 he set out in much fear and trembling to pay a visit to IDaniel Shubotham, a cousin of his, and a ringleader lin wickedness with whom he had held previous con- versations. Concerning this Christmas visit, Bourne says, "My natural timdity pressed upon me so that it ' was a task to go, but my mouth had been opened , before the Lord, and to have drawn back would have been awful; so I set off, taking with me a book written by R. Barclay, the Quaker, and I took the written account of my conversion and experience." After ' conversation Shubotham accompanied him on the way I home. "So soon as we were in a suitable place,' says Bourne, "I set to preaching the Gospel to him with all my might. At parting I put into his hands the full account of my conversion and experience." Bourne's heart was heavy when he took leave of his kinsman, for he feared that no good whatever had been done. But in this he was singularly mistaken, for Shubotham afterwards confessed that that morning every word went through him." A revival of religion at Harriseahead sprang • out of that Christmas morning's obedience. Shubotham began to preach with great success and stimulated even Bourne himself by his superior courage. Soon the face of the whole neighbourhood was changed. The revival spread until much of the country lying on the slopes and under the shadow of Mow Cop itself, was won for Christ. At the bottom of the hill, the colliers of Kidsgrove were brought under the revival spell. The work grew in Bourne's hands for he it was to whom everybody looked for guidance and counsel because of his book-learning and his reputation as a "safe man." "We had" he says "to establish order and maintain discipline, keep up the converting work, and promote piety.' He visited his converts in their homes and established a Society class. Now this revival moved on early Methodist lines. For a time, however, it remained unattached, or but slenderly attached to the official Methodism of the time. It was noted for the success of its "conversation-preaching" for all the converts followed Bourne's example in this respect. A great deal of "\button-holing " went on. Every man talked to his fellovr abut the new joyous experience. By impulse and on principle these new- born saints subjected their mates to the most impor- tunate personal appeal. Soon after the revival began a weekly cottage prayer-meeting was established at a good woman's house at Harriseahead, from which the sound of prayer and praise could be heard a mile and a half away. Let it not be thought, however, that there was no order in the meetings. Hugh Bourne was a man of unusual common sense. He would not allow the meetings to be held for more than an hour and a half at the longest, lest their occupations should suffer next day, and their good be evil spoken of. This restriction of time was a real hardship to those early stalwarts. One night, after an exceptionally good meeting expostulatory voices were heard: Would that the meeting had gone on longer !" " Why did you break it up so soon ?" they said, and it was then that Daniel Shubotham uttered a prophetic sentence when he replied "You shall have a meeting on Mow some 'Sunday, and have a whole day's praying, and then you'll be satisfied."

A few words must be written at this, point about the official Methodism of the time. Hugh Bourne, as we have seen, had joined the Methodist Church. But it must be recorded that the official Methodism of that day looked askance at not only this, but at other revivalistic movements in different parts of England. That explains why it was that during the period 1800-7 Hugh Bourne's name was never put on the Methodist plan, and why he and his co-workers were left severely alone. A second Revival in the district, due to the influ- ence of some Steckport Revivalists, is of momentous concern for Primitive Methodism, since it registered the conversion of William Clowes (the other main founder) which took place at Tunstall, whither the fire had spread. Like Bourne, Clowes had a humble origin. His birthplace was a workman's cottage in an obscure court at Burslem. Like him again, he had a worthless father, an indolent dissipated potter, who had been turned from his early religious inclinations by the reading of a pernicious book. Like Bourne, he was blessed with a good mother, but a mother who —despite her attachment to the Church of England— was herself in the dark, religiously, until after her son's conversion. And like Bourne, once more, William Clowes had a somewhat painful childhood. At ten years of age, he tells us, that, being at a prayer meeting he wept bitterly under the clear conviction of the sin of disobedience ; and later, and during a Revival at Burslein he adds : "My. convictions were such that had an experienced Christian taken me by the hand, I have no doubt that I should at that time have been converted; but being young I passed unnoticed and soon lost those convictions.' The result was that the first 20 years of Clowe's life are a warning to all who are called upon to train the young. The soil of his nature was rich indeed, but his parents sowed no good seed in it, and the weeds grew. His education was meagre, no intellectual interests were imparted to him. The world seemed fair, pleasure allured, and he went forth to meet it. His great accomplishment was dancing, and for this he had a perfect passion. Inevitably this led him into question- able places and bad company. "Associated with dancing was visiting public assembly rooms, where banquetings, gambling and fighting ranked among the sins of my youth," he writes. Drunkenness and profanity must be added to the black list. On one cccasion, during wake Week, he and his companions are actually found holding a mock prayer-meeting in the sanded parlour of a public-house at Leek. The year 1803 found him in Hull —well able to earn his pound a day as a potter—hut flinging in his lot with the press gangs of the times. Yet he had an earnest nature, for paroxysms of passion were succeeded by paroxysms of repentance and remorse. After returning to his native place a friend who knew of his anguish of soul took him to the House of God. Shortly after, he gained admission to a Love Feast. Seeing the bread and water carried round in the old-fashioned way, he thought "This must be the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper." The very idea of partaking made him feel that he was in danger of committing the unpardonable sin. Next morning he attended a prayer meeting, and wrestled. amid all the noise, as one alone with his Maker, until he felt that liberty was dawning. "What is this ? " he asked himself. "This is ;hat the Methodists mean by being converted: Yes, this is it —God is converting my soul. In an agony of prayer I believed God would save me—then I believed he was saving me—then I believed he had saved me, and it was so." , This great event took place in January 1805. The reality of the change was evident to all. Debts were paid. Old associations were broken off, and Clowes commenced a career of unremitting Christian toil He drew up strict rules for holy living, began to reprove sin, helped to suppress Sabbath-breaking, threw his house open for prayer-meetings, &c., and engaged in much evangelistic work in the homes of the people. •

At Cirencester on Thursday, William Henry Smart, grocer and Primitive Methodist local preacher. Ciren- cester, was remanded on a charge of obtaining £159 by false pretences, this being part of a sum of over £1,200 of which Smart was trustee of a widow, and the whole of which he is alleged to have drawn from the bank on the understanding that he would provide a better investment. The prisoner left by rail just before the hour at which he had promised to 'meet his co-trustee, and was subsequently apprehended. Bail was refused

THE ART MASTER'S POSITION. In face of the impending retirement of Mr. C. B. Aylward the School Management Committee recom- menaed that authority be given for an advertisement ; to be issued i nviting applications for the post of head- master of the School of Art, the remuneration to be a ; fixed salary at the rate of £225 per annum, together with a grant of 10s. for each paper, in excess of 125, worked by the students of the school at the Board of 1 Education's annual Art examinations; the total maximum :salary shall not exceed £3OO per annum, and that the bead-rwster devote his whole time to the service of the Committee, and that arrangements be made for the staff of the School of Art to give the art instruction at the Grammar Soho ol on one half day each week, M i the Com- mittee to receive the sum of t per annum n respect of such instruction. The minute was approved. RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION IN COUNCIL SCHOOLS. SCHEME DEFERRED. The School Management Committee submitted the proposed general regulations in respect of the religious instruction to be given in the Council schools. They recommended that in schools provided by the Com- mittee the Bible shall be read, and there shall be such explanations and instruction therefrom in the principles of Christian religion and of morality as are suited to the capacities of the children. The first half-hour of every morning and the last five or ten minutes of every afternoon's session of the school shall be devoted to such observances and instruc- tion. In the event of any parent or guardian objecting to his or her child being present during the time of Religious instruction, the child must be withdrawn and receive instruction in secular subjects in a separate room. The HeadiTescher shall arrant. that the Assistant Teacher who is responsible for tills securer instruction of any class shall also be responsible for the religious instructio n of the ,same class. The Head Teacher should, however, from time to time, take part in the actual instruction of the several classes, each of which he or she will be required to examine in Religious knowledge once in each year during the time set apart for Religious instruction, and shall enter the record of such examina- tion in the book provided for the purpose. The school is to be opened each morning with the singing of a hymn, the reading of a short portion of Scripture, and a prayer (in which all the teachers and scholars should join), after which the children separate to their classes for Religions Instruction. Five or ten minutes at the close of afternoon school are devoted to singing and wayer. The syllabus of instruction recommended was : Class I.—Learn the Lord's Prayer and Psalm xxiii. A brief account of the lives of Samuel and David. Leading facts in the life of our Lord told in simple language. ' Class IL—Learn the Lord's Prayer, Psalm xxiii. and the Ten Commandments. Exodus xx. 1-17. Learn St. Matther V., verses 1-12. Lessons from the life of Moses. Simple lessons from the life of our Lord. Class M.—Memory work as,,for Class H., learn St. Matthew xxii., verses 35-40, Psalm cxxi. Lessons from the lives of Samuel and David, together with the story of Ruth. Follow the account of the Life of our Lord, with lessons drawn from the following parables : The Talentti, the Good Samaritan, the Lost Sheep, the Lost piece of Money, the Prodigal Son, the Pharisee and the Publican. Class IV.—Memory work as for Class M., learn St. John xiv. verses 1-15 and Psalm cxxv. Lessons from the Pentateuch with special reference to the lives of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph and Moses, with the practical lessons to be derived therefrom. Lessons from the Gospel according to St. Luke 1-13. Class V.—Memory work as for Class IV., learn Corinthians 1., xii, verse Si and xiii., Psalms xxiii. and xci., Proverbs iii., verses 1-18 and xxiii. verses 20 and 21, and Romans xiii., verses 8-10. Lessons from the Book of Joshua. Lessons from the Gospel according to St. Luke xiv.-end. . Class VL—Memory work as for Class V., learn Psalms cxxi. and exxii. ; Isaiah lii. 13-15 Mi. ; Matthew xxii. 35-40. Lessons on the life and times of Elijah. Lessons from the Sermon on the Mount, St. Matthew v., vi. and vii. Lessons from the Gospel according to St. John L-xiii, Class Vll.—Memory work as for Class VI., learn Psalm xc., Isaiah lxi., and Hebrews i. Lessons from Isaiah i., vi., xi., xxv.. xxxv. and xl. Lessons from Matthew v., vi., vii. Lessons from the Gospel according. to St. John xiv-end. Study Acts of the Apos ties i.-xii Class VIII. —Repeat Class VII. work. learn Isaiah 1 and Psalms cxxv. and cxxvi. Study Acts of the Apostles xiii. nod xxviii. (take in Matthews letter) Mr.STerm said it would have been far better if copies of the proposed regulations had been forwarded to mem- bers of the Committee. They had not had an oppor- tunity of considering them and were not in a position that evening to discuss them. Mr. ROBERTS thought Mr. Steel's question was a very proper one and he thought it would be as sell if they adjourned the question of adopting the regulations until every member of the Committee had had an oppor- tunity of considering them. Personally,and spanking as a Nonconformist he was more than satisfied with the scheme and he thought the fact that there were Noncon- formists on the sub-committee ought to be accepted as proof there was nothing' in the regulations in the slightest calculated to offend in any shape or form. On the contrary he though it was a most happy arrange- ment, and would . commend itself to all reasonable minded men. Of course there were extremists even amongst Nonconformists, but be did not think thete was that occasion for offence, in the slightest, which their friend Mr. Alatthees had set out to discover. Canon STEVENSON explainod that copies of the regula- tions had not been circulated in .order to save the cost of printing. The matter was really one for the school managers but having regard to the fact that the Coun- cil school was a new one the managers had been most careful to report every action of importance. He with. drew the recommendations in order thet the members of the Committee could have an opportunity of fully dis- cussing them. .Mr. BURGESS urged that it was a matter for the Com- mittee as the regulations applied to the Council Schools and not only to the Beamont School. Mr. KINGDON asked if the managers of other schools would have power to alter the scheme. Canon STEvESSON : . Not if this Committee approves it.
